title: III. Dislocation densities in some annealed and cold-worked metals from measurements on the X-ray debye-scherrer spectrum
abstract: Abstract Two basic equations are derived for deducing the dislocation density in powdered materials from the particle size and strain breadth measured from the Debye-Schemer spectrum. In the particle size estimate, it is assumed that the material has a block structure similar to that found in microbeam studies and that the dislocations lie along the block surfaces. The number of dislocations along each face, n, is not known. In the strain broadening estimate the x-ray line broadening from a dislocation array is calculated in terms of the broadening due to an isolated dislocation and a strain energy factor F, which allows for the effect of dislocation arrangement. Both methods involve an unknown quantity but by equating the two results it is possible in most cases to get both a narrow bracket for the dislocation density and considerable information on the dislocation arrangement. In annealed metals the values of p range from 2 × 107 cm of dislocation line per cm3 for aluminium to 3 × 108 for tungsten and molybdenum, the majority of dislocations being 'random', i.e. the number along each edge is approximately 1. There is some correlation between p and the purity and annealing treatment of the powder. High purity and high annealing temperatures result in smaller dislocation densities. In cold-worked metals the dislocation density is more variable. A precise analysis is possible for aluminium; high purity aluminium filed at room temperature gives p=4·5 to 7·6 × 109 with evidence for recovery, possibly by polygonization. Commercially pure aluminium filed at both room temperature and liquid air give p = 5 × 109 to 2·7 × 1010 and p = 1·5 × 1010 to 3·2 × 1011 respectively. Some dislocation array such as a 'pile-up', which causes an increase in the strain energy of dislocations exists in both these samples as with all the other metals examined. Dislocation densities are also given for tungsten, molybdenum, iron and α-brass. In α-brass, the only alloy considered, p is higher than for the pure metals and there is strong evidence that the dislocations are effectively random and that each dislocation is attached to a stacking fault.
summary:
Scientific Paper Breakdown: Dislocation Densities in Metals Analyzed
--------------------------------------------------------------

Researchers G.K. Williamson and R.E. Smallman, publishing in the *Philosophical Magazine*, propose a novel approach to measure dislocation densities in various metals using X-ray Debye-Scherrer spectra. This study builds upon prior work in materials science, particularly focusing on understanding dislocations — imperfections within crystal structures — and their role in material properties.

The paper presents two methods for estimating the dislocation density based on particle size and strain broadening derived from X-ray diffraction data. The scientists aim to create a narrow bracket for the dislocation densities, offering insights into these materials' substructures and dislocation arrangements.

In annealed metals such as aluminum, tungsten, and molybdenum, the dislocation density findings vary significantly, with values ranging from 2 × 10^7 cm³ of dislocation line per cm³ in aluminum to 3 × 10^8 for tungsten and molybdenum. The study indicates that dislocations in the majority of cases are 'random,' meaning there's approximately one dislocation along each edge.

The researchers found a correlation between dislocation density (p) and the purity and annealing treatment of the powder, with higher purity and temperature resulting in smaller dislocation densities. In cold-worked metals, dislocation densities are more variable, with precise analyses being possible for aluminum, particularly high-purity samples filed at room temperature, where p ranges from 4.5 × 10^9 to 7.6 × 10^9, suggesting evidence of recovery, possibly by polygonization.

Additional dislocation density data is provided for tungsten, molybdenum, iron, and alpha-brass, with the latter displaying higher dislocation densities than pure metals, hinting at effectively random dislocations and stacking faults within the alloy structure. The study offers valuable insights into the dislocation dynamics of various materials, enabling a better understanding of material properties in solid-state physics and improving material design and manufacturing processes.

title: Helical Liquids and Majorana Bound States in Quantum Wires
abstract: We show that the combination of spin-orbit coupling with a Zeeman field or strong interactions may lead to the formation of a helical electron liquid in single-channel quantum wires, with spin and velocity perfectly correlated. We argue that zero-energy Majorana bound states are formed in various situations when such wires are situated in proximity to a conventional s-wave superconductor. This occurs when the external magnetic field, the superconducting gap, or, most simply, the chemical potential vary along the wire. These Majorana states do not require the presence of a vortex in the system. Experimental consequences of the helical liquid and the Majorana states are also discussed.
summary:
Title: New research advances in Majorana physics finds helical electron liquids

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers Yuval Oreg, Gil Refael, and Felix von Oppen have explored the formation of a unique state of matter known as a "helical electron liquid" in single-channel quantum wires. By combining spin-orbit coupling with a Zeeman field or strong interactions, they found that this state results in perfect correlation between spin and velocity, shedding light on new possibilities for Majorana bound states.

The researchers argue that the presence of zero-energy Majorana bound states can be observed under various conditions when such wires are situated near conventional s-wave superconductors. Notably, their study suggests that these Majorana states do not require a vortex within the system, potentially simplifying future experimental setups to investigate this intriguing phenomenon's properties further. Experimental consequences and implications of the helical electron liquid and Majorana states serve as avenues for further exploration in condensed matter physics.

title: Quantized conductance of point contacts in a two-dimensional electron gas
abstract: Ballistic point contacts, defined in the two-dimensional electron gas of a GaAs-AlGaAs heterostructure, have been studied in zero magnetic field. The conductance changes in quantized steps of e2/πħ when the width, controlled by a gate on top of the heterojunction, is varied. Up to sixteen steps are observed when the point contact is widened from 0 to 360 nm. An explanation is proposed, which assumes quantized transverse momentum in the point-contact region.

title: Coherent Manipulation of Coupled Electron Spins in Semiconductor Quantum Dots
abstract: We demonstrated coherent control of a quantum two-level system based on two-electron spin states in a double quantum dot, allowing state preparation, coherent manipulation, and projective readout. These techniques are based on rapid electrical control of the exchange interaction. Separating and later recombining a singlet spin state provided a measurement of the spin dephasing time, T 2 *, of ∼10 nanoseconds, limited by hyperfine interactions with the gallium arsenide host nuclei. Rabi oscillations of two-electron spin states were demonstrated, and spin-echo pulse sequences were used to suppress hyperfine-induced dephasing. Using these quantum control techniques, a coherence time for two-electron spin states exceeding 1 microsecond was observed.
summary:

The study's focus centers on the suppression of dephasing, a crucial concept in quantum mechanics that degrades the coherence time of quantum states. Using their techniques, the scientists were able to observe a two-electron spin coherence time surpassing 1 microsecond, marking significant progress in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Reversible Electrical Switching Phenomena in Disordered Structures
abstract: A rapid and reversible transition between a highly resistive and conductive state effected by an electric field, which we have observed in various types of disordered semiconducting material, is described in detail. The switching parameters and chemical composition of a typical material are presented, and microscopic mechanisms for the conduction phenomena are suggested.
summary:
New Materials Discovery Offers Reversible electrical Switching:

Physicist Stanford Ovshinsky's groundbreaking research published in Physical Review Letters shows the possibility of rapidly reversible switching between highly resistive and conductive states in disordered semiconducting materials, a finding that could revolutionize electronic devices. The study presents the parameters and chemical composition of a typical material and proposes microscopic mechanisms for this conduction phenomenon. This work builds upon the broader area of materials science, adding crucial insights into thermal conduction, electrical conductors, electric fields, and disordered structures.

title: Correlated electrons in high-temperature superconductors
abstract:
Theoretical ideas and experimental results concerning high temperature
superconductors are reviewed. Special emphasis is given to calculations carried
out with the help of computers applied to models of strongly correlated
electrons proposed to describe the two dimensional ${\rm Cu O_2}$ planes. The
review also includes results using several analytical techniques. The one and
three band Hubbard models, and the ${\rm t-J}$ model are discussed, and their
behavior compared against experiments when available. Among the conclusions of
the review, we found that some experimentally observed unusual properties of
the cuprates have a natural explanation through Hubbard-like models. In
particular abnormal features like the mid-infrared band of the optical
conductivity $\sigma(\omega)$, the new states observed in the gap in
photoemission experiments, the behavior of the spin correlations with doping,
and the presence of phase separation in the copper oxide superconductors may be
explained, at least in part, by these models. Finally, the existence of
superconductivity in Hubbard-like models is analyzed. Some aspects of the
recently proposed ideas to describe the cuprates as having a $\dx2y2$
superconducting condensate at low temperatures are discussed. Numerical results
favor this scenario over others....(continues).
summary:
Title: "High-temperature superconductors explained through 'Hubbard model' review"

Headline: Cutting-edge research shines light on cuprate superconductors using computer simulations and Hubbard models

Summary: In an article published in Reviews of Modern Physics, author Elbio Dagotto reviews the latest theoretical ideas and experimental results regarding high-temperature superconductors. The focus lies on calculations done with strongly correlated electron models specifically proposed to describe the cuprate's two-dimensional ${\rm Cu O_2}$ planes. Results from one and three-band Hubbard models, as well as the t-J model, are discussed and compared against experiments when possible. Key findings include that various unusual properties of the cuprates might be explicated by these Hubbard-like models, such as anomalous features like the mid-infrared band of the optical conductivity, new states observed in photoemission experiments, spin correlations with doping, and the presence of phase separation in copper oxide superconductors. Further analysis reveals the potential existence of superconductivity in Hubbard-like models and sheds light on recently proposed concepts to describe cuprates like having a ${\rm dx2y2}$ superconducting condensate at low temperatures.

title: First-principles calculations for defects and impurities: Applications to III-nitrides
abstract: First-principles calculations have evolved from mere aids in explaining and supporting experiments to powerful tools for predicting new materials and their properties. In the first part of this review we describe the state-of-the-art computational methodology for calculating the structure and energetics of point defects and impurities in semiconductors. We will pay particular attention to computational aspects which are unique to defects or impurities, such as how to deal with charge states and how to describe and interpret transition levels. In the second part of the review we will illustrate these capabilities with examples for defects and impurities in nitride semiconductors. Point defects have traditionally been considered to play a major role in wide-band-gap semiconductors, and first-principles calculations have been particularly helpful in elucidating the issues. Specifically, calculations have shown that the unintentional n-type conductivity that has often been observed in as-grown GaN cannot be attributed to nitrogen vacancies, but is due to unintentional incorporation of donor impurities. Native point defects may play a role in compensation and in phenomena such as the yellow luminescence, which can be attributed to gallium vacancies. In the section on impurities, specific attention will be focused on dopants. Oxygen, which is commonly present as a contaminant, is a shallow donor in GaN but becomes a deep level in AlGaN due to a DX transition. Magnesium is almost universally used as the p-type dopant, but hole concentrations are still limited. Reasons for this behavior are discussed, and alternative acceptors are examined. Hydrogen plays an important role in p-type GaN, and the mechanisms that underlie its behavior are explained. Incorporating hydrogen along with acceptors is an example of codoping; a critical discussion of codoping is presented. Most of the information available to date for defects and impurities in nitrides has been generated for GaN, but we will also discuss AlN and InN where appropriate. We conclude by summarizing the main points and looking towards the future.
summary:
**Science Article Headline:**
"First-principles calculations illuminate key role of defects and impurities in III-nitride semiconductors"

**Article Summary:**
In a new review published in the Journal of Applied Physics, authors Chris G. Van de Walle and Jörg Neugebauer explore the latest computational methodology for understanding point defects and impurities in semiconductors, with a focus on nitride materials like Gallium Nitride (GaN), Aluminum Gallium Nitrate (AlGaN), Aluminum Nitride (AlN), and Indium Nitride (InN).

The authors demonstrate how these first-principles calculations have evolved, not just as aids for experiments, but powerful tools capable of predicting new materials and their properties. The study finds that native point defects can significantly impact the conductivity and behavior of wide-bandgap semiconductors like GaN, shedding light on phenomena such as yellow luminescence and unintentional n-type conductivity in as-grown GaN.

Particular emphasis was placed on understanding the roles of important impurities like oxygen, magnesium, and hydrogen, which can impact doping behavior and overall semiconductor performance. The authors also discuss codoping -- the intentional incorporation of more than one element in a crystal structure -- as a critical process for designing next-generation nitride semiconductors with enhanced properties.

title: The instability of liquid surfaces when accelerated in a direction perpendicular to their planes. I
abstract: Abstract It is shown that, when two superposed fluids of different densities are accelerated in a direction perpendicular to their interface, this surface is stable or unstable according to whether the acceleration is directed from the heavier to the lighter fluid or vice versa. The relationship between the rate of development of the instability and the length of wave-like disturbances, the acceleration and the densities is found, and similar calculations are made for the case when a sheet of liquid of uniform depth is accelerated.
summary:
New physics research reveals surprising insights about the stability of fluid surfaces under perpendicular acceleration

Geoffrey Ingram Taylor's groundbreaking study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A Mathematical and Physical Sciences, explores the instability of liquid surfaces when subjected to acceleration perpendicular to their planes. The work builds upon previous research in mechanics and physics by investigating the behavior of two superposed fluids of different densities being accelerated in opposite directions. Taylor finds that the surface is stable or unstable depending on whether the acceleration is directed from the heavier to the lighter fluid or vice versa. This discovery offers vital insights into fluid dynamics, potentially leading to advancements in various areas where liquids are accelerated perpendicularly.

title: Nanoscale thermal transport
abstract: Rapid progress in the synthesis and processing of materials with structure on nanometer length scales has created a demand for greater scientific understanding of thermal transport in nanoscale devices, individual nanostructures, and nanostructured materials. This review emphasizes developments in experiment, theory, and computation that have occurred in the past ten years and summarizes the present status of the field. Interfaces between materials become increasingly important on small length scales. The thermal conductance of many solid–solid interfaces have been studied experimentally but the range of observed interface properties is much smaller than predicted by simple theory. Classical molecular dynamics simulations are emerging as a powerful tool for calculations of thermal conductance and phonon scattering, and may provide for a lively interplay of experiment and theory in the near term. Fundamental issues remain concerning the correct definitions of temperature in nonequilibrium nanoscale systems. Modern Si microelectronics are now firmly in the nanoscale regime—experiments have demonstrated that the close proximity of interfaces and the extremely small volume of heat dissipation strongly modifies thermal transport, thereby aggravating problems of thermal management. Microelectronic devices are too large to yield to atomic-level simulation in the foreseeable future and, therefore, calculations of thermal transport must rely on solutions of the Boltzmann transport equation; microscopic phonon scattering rates needed for predictive models are, even for Si, poorly known. Low-dimensional nanostructures, such as carbon nanotubes, are predicted to have novel transport properties; the first quantitative experiments of the thermal conductivity of nanotubes have recently been achieved using microfabricated measurement systems. Nanoscale porosity decreases the permittivity of amorphous dielectrics but porosity also strongly decreases the thermal conductivity. The promise of improved thermoelectric materials and problems of thermal management of optoelectronic devices have stimulated extensive studies of semiconductor superlattices; agreement between experiment and theory is generally poor. Advances in measurement methods, e.g., the 3ω method, time-domain thermoreflectance, sources of coherent phonons, microfabricated test structures, and the scanning thermal microscope, are enabling new capabilities for nanoscale thermal metrology.
summary:
Headline: Advances in Nanoscale Thermal Transport Key to Future Microelectronics

Summary: A comprehensive review published in the Journal of Applied Physics highlights the rapid growth in nanotechnology and its impact on thermal transport within small devices, individual nanostructures, and materials. The study underscores developments in experimentation, theory, and computation over the past decade regarding thermal conductivity, interfaces between materials and phonon scattering. As modern microelectronics transition into the nanoscale regime, issues surrounding temperature definitions, atomic-level simulating, and thermal management become more critical. Notable topics discussed include the thermal properties of carbon nanotubes, porosity effects on amorphous dielectrics, semiconductor superlattices, and recent advancements in measurement techniques for nanoscale thermal metrology.

title: Model for Lattice Thermal Conductivity at Low Temperatures
abstract: A phenomenological model is developed to facilitate calculation of lattice thermal conductivities at low temperatures. It is assumed that the phonon scattering processes can be represented by frequency-dependent relaxation times. Isotropy and absence of dispersion in the crystal vibration spectrum are assumed. No distinction is made between longitudinal and transverse phonons. The assumed scattering mechanisms are (1) point impurities (isotopes), (2) normal three-phonon processes, (3) umklapp processes, and (4) boundary scattering. A special investigation is made of the role of the normal processes which conserve the total crystal momentum and a formula is derived from the Boltzmann equation which gives their contribution to the conductivity. The relaxation time for the normal three-phonon processes is taken to be that calculated by Herring for longitudinal modes in cubic materials. The model predicts for germanium a thermal conductivity roughly proportional to ${T}^{\ensuremath{-}\frac{3}{2}}$ in normal material, but proportional to ${T}^{\ensuremath{-}2}$ in single-isotope material in the temperature range 50\ifmmode^\circ\else\textdegree\fi{}-100\ifmmode^\circ\else\textdegree\fi{}K. Magnitudes of the relaxation times are estimated from the experimental data. The thermal conductivity of germanium is calculated by numerical integration for the temperature range 2-100\ifmmode^\circ\else\textdegree\fi{}K. The results are in reasonably good agreement with the experimental results for normal and for single-isotope material.
summary: In a breakthrough for condensed matter physics, a new model for the thermal conductivity at low temperatures is proposed by physicist J. Callaway, published in Physical Review. The model, built upon ideas of phonons and several scattering mechanisms, aims to streamline calculations of thermal conductivities within non-dispersive crystals, assuming that phonon scattering processes can be represented by frequency-dependent relaxation times. This model has implications for materials like germanium, predicting thermal conductivity proportionate to T^-3/2 in standard materials and T^-2 in single-isotope materials between 50°K and 100°K. Results show good agreement with experimental data, opening new avenues for understanding and manipulating heat transfer in solids.
allAuthors: J. Callaway

title: Anomalous transit-time dispersion in amorphous solids
abstract: Measurements of the transient photocurrent $I(t)$ in an increasing number of inorganic and organic amorphous materials display anomalous transport properties. The long tail of $I(t)$ indicates a dispersion of carrier transit times. However, the shape invariance of $I(t)$ to electric field and sample thickness (designated as universality for the classes of materials here considered) is incompatible with traditional concepts of statistical spreading, i.e., a Gaussian carrier packet. We have developed a stochastic transport model for $I(t)$ which describes the dynamics of a carrier packet executing a time-dependent random walk in the presence of a field-dependent spatial bias and an absorbing barrier at the sample surface. The time dependence of the random walk is governed by hopping time distribution $\ensuremath{\Psi}(t)$. A packet, generated with a $\ensuremath{\Psi}(t)$ characteristic of hopping in a disordered system [e.g., $\ensuremath{\Psi}(t)\ensuremath{\sim}{t}^{\ensuremath{-}(1+\ensuremath{\alpha})}$, $0<\ensuremath{\alpha}<1$], is shown to propagate with a number of anomalous non-Gaussian properties. The calculated $I(t)$ associated with this packet not only obeys the property of universality but can account quantitatively for a large variety of experiments. The new method of data analysis advanced by the theory allows one to directly extract the transit time even for a featureless current trace. In particular, we shall analyze both an inorganic ($a\ensuremath{-}{\mathrm{As}}_{2}{\mathrm{Se}}_{3}$) and an organic (trinitrofluorenone-polyvinylcarbazole) system. Our function $\ensuremath{\Psi}(t)$ is related to a first-principles calculation. It is to be emphasized that these $\ensuremath{\Psi}(t)$'s characterize a realization of a non-Markoffian transport process. Moreover, the theory shows the limitations of the concept of a mobility in this dispersive type of transport.
summary:
New Study Sheds Light on Anomalous Transport Properties in Amorphous Solids

Physicists H. Scher and Elliott W. Montroll have developed a groundbreaking model to explain anomalous transit-time dispersion in various inorganic and organic amorphous materials, challenging traditional concepts of statistical spreading. The researchers' new stochastic transport model describes the dynamics of a carrier packet executing a time-dependent random walk in the presence of a field-dependent spatial bias and an absorbing barrier, providing a quantitative explanation for several experiments in amorphous solids.

Their study demonstrates that non-Gaussian properties, such as universality observed across electric fields and sample thicknesses, can be attributed to hopping time distribution $\Psi(t)$ that characterizes dispersive transport processes in disordered systems. By applying this new method of data analysis, the researchers were able to directly extract the transit times from featureless current traces, providing an innovative approach for understanding these materials' unique properties.

In their work, they analyze both an inorganic ($a$-As2Se3) and an organic (trinitrofluorenone-polyvinylcarbazole) system, further emphasizing the significance of their findings by relating $\Psi(t)$ to first-principles calculations. The study uncovers limitations in the concept of mobility for this dispersive type of transport, offering important insights into the field of physics and amorphous solids research.

title: Spin Hall Effect
abstract:
It is proposed that when a charge current circulates in a paramagnetic metal
a transverse spin imbalance will be generated, giving rise to a 'spin Hall
voltage'. Similarly, that when a spin current circulates a transverse charge
imbalance will be generated, hence a Hall voltage, in the absence of charge
current and magnetic field. Based on these principles we propose an experiment
to generate and detect a spin current in a paramagnetic metal.
summary:
Scientist Proposes New Spin Hall Effect Theory for Paramagnetic Metals

In a newly published paper by J. E. Hirsch in Physical Review Letters, the researcher proposes a groundbreaking theory that could revolutionize the field of Condensed Matter Physics. The theory, known as the Spin Hall Effect, suggests that circulating charge currents in paramagnetic metals can generate a 'spin imbalance', creating a potential source for 'spin Hall voltage'.

Similarly, the theory posits that circulating spin currents can generate a transverse charge imbalance, leading to a Hall voltage even in the absence of conventional charge current and magnetic fields. This novel concept could pave the way for exploring new ways to produce and detect spin currents in paramagnetic metals.

title: Room-Temperature Quantum Hall Effect in Graphene
abstract: The quantum Hall effect (QHE), one example of a quantum phenomenon that occurs on a truly macroscopic scale, has attracted intense interest since its discovery in 1980 and has helped elucidate many important aspects of quantum physics. It has also led to the establishment of a new metrological standard, the resistance quantum. Disappointingly, however, the QHE has been observed only at liquid-helium temperatures. We show that in graphene, in a single atomic layer of carbon, the QHE can be measured reliably even at room temperature, which makes possible QHE resistance standards becoming available to a broader community, outside a few national institutions.
summary:
**Groundbreaking discovery: Quantum Hall Effect observed at room temperature in graphene**

In a remarkable breakthrough, scientists have achieved what was once considered impossible - observing the quantum Hall effect (QHE) at room temperature using graphene, a single atomic layer of carbon. This finding, published in Science, could revolutionize the study of the QHE as it makes this phenomenon more accessible to a broader scientific community outside of a few national institutions.

Since its discovery in 1980, the quantum Hall effect has been a subject of intense research due to its unique properties and contributions to understanding quantum physics. However, it has always required liquid-helium temperatures for observation. This latest development marks a significant step forward in the field, potentially paving the way for new metrological standards based on the QHE resistance.

title: Approaching ballistic transport in suspended graphene.
abstract: The discovery of graphene raises the prospect of a new class of nanoelectronic devices based on the extraordinary physical properties of this one-atom-thick layer of carbon. Unlike two-dimensional electron layers in semiconductors, where the charge carriers become immobile at low densities, the carrier mobility in graphene can remain high, even when their density vanishes at the Dirac point. However, when the graphene sample is supported on an insulating substrate, potential fluctuations induce charge puddles that obscure the Dirac point physics. Here we show that the fluctuations are significantly reduced in suspended graphene samples and we report low-temperature mobility approaching 200,000 cm2 V-1 s-1 for carrier densities below 5 x 109 cm-2. Such values cannot be attained in semiconductors or non-suspended graphene. Moreover, unlike graphene samples supported by a substrate, the conductivity of suspended graphene at the Dirac point is strongly dependent on temperature and approaches ballistic values at liquid helium temperatures. At higher temperatures, above 100 K, we observe the onset of thermally induced long-range scattering.
summary:
New study in Nature Nanotechnology uncovers high carrier mobility in suspended graphene

In a groundbreaking discovery, scientists have found that suspended graphene, a one-atom thick layer of carbon, outperforms semiconductors in terms of carrier mobility at low densities. Unlike traditional two-dimensional electron layers in semiconductors where charge carriers become immobile at low densities, the carrier mobility in graphene can remain high even when their density vanishes at the Dirac point. The research, led by Xu Du and colleagues, reveals that potential fluctuations, which obscure the Dirac point physics in supported graphene samples, are significantly reduced in suspended graphene. This has led to low-temperature mobility approaching 200,000 cm² V-1 s-1 for carrier densities below 5 x 109 cm-2 and could potentially revolutionize nanoelectronics.

The research builds upon the extraordinary physical properties of graphene and the potential for new classes of nanoelectronic devices. It also supports the idea that suspended graphene offers unique advantages over supported graphene, particularly in terms of ballistic transport at low temperatures.

title: Polarons in crystalline and non-crystalline materials
abstract: Abstract The current state of polaron theory as applicable to transition metal oxides is reviewed, including problems such as impurity conduction where disorder plays a role. An estimate is given of the conditions under which polaron formation leads to an enhancement of the mass but no hopping energy. The binding energy of a polaron to a donor or acceptor in narrow-band semiconductors is discussed. The experimental evidence about the conductivity of TiO2 and NiO is reviewed. Impurity conduction in NiO and conduction in glasses containing transition metal ions is discussed and it is emphasized that the activation energy for hopping nearly all vanishes at low temperatures. Pollak's theory of a.c. impurity conductivity is reviewed and applied to the problem of dielectric loss in these materials.
summary:
**Article Headline:**
"Review uncovers key insights into polaron behavior in transition metal oxides, improving understanding of thermal conduction"

**Summary:**
In a comprehensive review published in Advances In Physics, researchers I.G. Austin and N.F. Mott explore the current state of "polaron" theory, focusing on transition metal oxides – a critical area within condensed matter physics. The paper delves into issues such as impurity conduction where disorder plays a significant role. It provides estimates for conditions under which polaron formation leads to enhanced mass but no hopping energy. Furthermore, the authors discuss the binding energy of polarons to donors or acceptors in narrow-band semiconductors. The experimental evidence on the conductivity of TiO2 and NiO is reviewed, along with impurity conduction in NiO and conductivity in glasses containing transition metal ions. Notably, they emphasize that the activation energy for hopping tends to vanish at low temperatures. Additionally, the paper reviews Pollak's theory of a.c. impurity conduction and applies it to explain dielectric loss in these materials, offering valuable insights into the field of condensed matter physics.

title: Plasma Losses by Fast Electrons in Thin Films
abstract: The angle-energy distribution of a fast electron losing energy to the conduction electrons in a thick metallic foil has been derived assuming that the conduction electrons constitute a Fermi-Dirac gas and that the fast electron undergoes only small fractional energy and momentum changes. This distribution exhibits both collective interaction characteristics and individual interaction characteristics, and is more general than the result obtained by other workers. Describing the conduction electrons by the hydro-dynamical equations of Bloch, it has been shown that for very thin idealized foils energy loss may occur at a value which is less than the plasma energy, while as the foil thickness decreases below $\ensuremath{\sim}\frac{v}{{\ensuremath{\omega}}_{p}}$ the loss at the plasma energy becomes less than that predicted by more conventional theories. The net result is an increase in the energy loss per unit thickness as the foil thickness is decreased. It is suggested that the predicted loss at subplasma energies may correspond to some of the low-lying energy losses which have been observed by experimenters using thin foils.
summary:
New Study on Electron Energy Loss in Thin Films Challenges Previous Findings

In a groundbreaking paper published in Physical Review, author R.H. Ritchie challenges previous theories on plasma energy loss in thin films. The research, centered around atomic physics, introduces a more comprehensive angle-energy distribution of fast electrons losing energy to conduction electrons in thick metallic foils.

Ritchie's model assumes the conduction electrons behave as a Fermi-Dirac gas and focuses on small energy and momentum changes for the fast electron, resulting in a distribution that exhibits both collective and individual interaction characteristics. This new approach is more general than earlier results, particularly when describing very thin foils where energy loss can occur below the plasma energy—a finding that contradicts conventional theories.

The study suggests that the predicted low-energy losses observed by experimentalists using thin films may correspond to this novel subplasma energy loss phenomenon. In essence, Ritchie's work offers a fresh perspective on energy transfer mechanisms in thin film physics, offering potential implications for various industries relying on such materials.

abstract:
The $La_{1-x} Sr_x MnO_3$ system with $0.2 \lesssim x \lesssim 0.4$ has
traditionally been modelled with a ``double exchange'' Hamiltonian, in which it
is assumed that the only relevant physics is the tendency of carrier hopping to
line up neighboring spins. We present a solution of the double exchange model,
show it is incompatible with many aspects of the resistivity data, and propose
that a strong electron-phonon interaction arising from a Jahn-Teller splitting
of the outer Mn d-level plays a crucial role.
summary:
Headline:
New Study Challenges Traditional Model for Resistivity in $La_{1-x} Sr_x MnO_3$: Strong Electron-Phonon Interaction Found Crucial

Summary:
Physicists A. J. Millis, P. B. Littlewood, and Boris I. Shraiman challenge a longstanding assumption about the $La_{1-x} Sr_x MnO_3$ system's resistivity. The traditional "double exchange" model, which focuses on carrier hopping aligning neighboring spins, is shown to disagree with much of the resistance data. Instead, the team suggests a significant electron-phonon interaction stemming from a Jahn-Teller splitting of the outer Mn d-level plays a key role in this material's properties (Physical Review Letters, 2023).

title: Effects of Double Exchange in Magnetic Crystals
abstract: This paper discusses some effects of mobile electrons in some antiferromagnetic lattices. It is shown that these electrons (or holes) always give rise to a distortion of the ground state spin arrangement, since electron transfer lowers the energy by a term of first order in the distortion angles. In the most typical cases this results in: (a) a nonzero spontaneous moment in low fields; (b) a lack of saturation in high fields; (c) simultaneous occurrence of "ferromagnetic" and "antiferromagnetic" lines in neutron diffraction patterns; (d) both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic branches in the spin wave spectra. Some of these properties have indeed been observed in compounds of mixed valency such as the manganites with low ${\mathrm{Mn}}^{4+}$ content. Similar considerations apply at finite temperatures, at least for the (most widespread) case where only the bottom of the carrier band is occupied at all temperatures of interest. The free energy is computed by a variational procedure, using simple carrier wave functions and an extension of the molecular field approximation. It is found that the canted arrangements are stable up to a well-defined temperature ${T}_{1}$. Above ${T}_{1}$ the system is either antiferromagnetic or ferromagnetic, depending upon the relative amount of mobile electrons. This behavior is not qualitatively modified when the carriers which are responsible for double exchange fall into bound states around impurity ions of opposite charge. Such bound states, however, will give rise to local inhomogeneities in the spin distortion, and to diffuse magnetic peaks in the neutron diffraction pattern. The possibility of observing these peaks and of eliminating the spurious spin-wave scattering is discussed in an Appendix.
summary:
"Physicist P. G. de Gennes Explores Electronic Distortions in Antiferromagnetic Crystals"

In a new paper published in Physical Review, French physicist P. G. de Gennes delves into the effects of mobile electrons in certain antiferromagnetic lattices. He finds that these mobile electrons (or holes) cause a distortion in the ground state spin arrangement, leading to several distinctive properties like nonzero spontaneous moments, lack of saturation in high fields, simultaneous occurrence of "ferromagnetic" and "antiferromagnetic" lines in neutron diffraction patterns, and both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic branches in the spin wave spectra.

These unique properties have been observed in compounds with low Mn4+ content, such as manganites. De Gennes' research also suggests that this behavior persists, even when the carriers responsible for double exchange fall into bound states around impurity ions of opposite charge. He further discusses the potential for observing these magnetic peaks in neutron diffraction patterns and eliminating spurious spin-wave scattering.

title: Improvements to NOAA’s Historical Merged Land–Ocean Surface Temperature Analysis (1880–2006)
abstract: Abstract Observations of sea surface and land–near-surface merged temperature anomalies are used to monitor climate variations and to evaluate climate simulations; therefore, it is important to make analyses of these data as accurate as possible. Analysis uncertainty occurs because of data errors and incomplete sampling over the historical period. This manuscript documents recent improvements in NOAA’s merged global surface temperature anomaly analysis, monthly, in spatial 5° grid boxes. These improvements allow better analysis of temperatures throughout the record, with the greatest improvements in the late nineteenth century and since 1985. Improvements in the late nineteenth century are due to improved tuning of the analysis methods. Beginning in 1985, improvements are due to the inclusion of bias-adjusted satellite data. The old analysis (version 2) was documented in 2005, and this improved analysis is called version 3.
summary:
Scientific Breakthrough: New NOAA Analysis Enhances Sea Surface Temperature Data

In a recent study published in the Journal of Climate, researchers led by Thomas M. Smith have made significant improvements to NOAA's Historical Merged Land–Ocean Surface Temperature Analysis. The team aims to increase the accuracy of sea surface and land-near surface temperature anomalies used for monitoring climate variations and evaluating climate simulations.

The advancements address analysis uncertainty caused by data errors and incomplete sampling over the historical period. Important improvements have been achieved, particularly in the late 19th century and since 1985. These enhancements were made through better tuning of analysis methods for older data and the inclusion of bias-adjusted satellite data for more recent years. The new, improved analysis is referred to as version 3, which updates an earlier version (version 2) documented in 2005. This progressive research paves the way for a clearer understanding of climate changes in the past and present.

title: Spontaneous polarization and piezoelectric constants of III-V nitrides
abstract:
The spontaneous polarization, dynamical Born charges, and piezoelectric
constants of the III-V nitrides AlN, GaN, and InN are studied ab initio using
the Berry phase approach to polarization in solids. The piezoelectric constants
are found to be up 10 times larger than in conventional III-V's and II-VI's,
and comparable to those of ZnO. Further properties at variance with those of
conventional III-V compounds are the sign of the piezoelectric constants
(positive as in II-VI's) and the very large spontaneous polarization.
summary:
Title: Groundbreaking Study Unveils Larger Piezoelectric Constants in III-V Nitrides

The research paper, "Spontaneous polarization and piezoelectric constants of III-V nitrides" published in Physical Review. B, Condensed Matter, presents an intriguing discovery by authors Fabio Bernardini, Vincenzo Fiorentini, and David Vanderbilt. The study focuses on Piezoelectricity, a crucial concept bridging the fields of physics and materials science.

This work builds upon the understanding of conventional III-V semiconductors and II-VI compounds by revealing that the piezoelectric constants in AlN, GaN, and InN - a class of III-V nitrides - are up to 10 times larger than their counterparts. The findings equate these constituents to ZnO, further challenging our understanding of III-V semiconductors and opening new possibilities for their utilization in various fields. The study also underlines differences such as the positive sign of the piezoelectric constants, akin to II-VI compounds, and unusually large spontaneous polarizations, distinct from conventional III-V compounds.

title: Considerations on Double Exchange
abstract: Zener has suggested a type of interaction between the spins of magnetic ions which he named "double exchange." This occurs indirectly by means of spin coupling to mobile electrons which travel from one ion to the next. We have calculated this interaction for a pair of ions with general spin $S$ and with general transfer integral, $b$, and internal exchange integral $J$.One result is that while the states of large total spin have both the highest and lowest energies, their average energy is the same as for the states of low total spin. This should be applicable in the high-temperature expansion of the susceptibility, and if it is, indicates that the high-temperature Curie-Weiss constant $\ensuremath{\theta}$ should be zero, and $\frac{1}{\ensuremath{\chi}}$ vs $T$ a curved line. This is surprising in view of the fact that the manganites, in which double exchange has been presumed to be the interaction mechanism, obey a fairly good Curie-Weiss law.The results can be approximated rather well by a simple semiclassical model in which the spins of the ion cores are treated classically. This model is capable of rather easy extension to the problem of the whole crystal, but the resulting mathematical problem is not easily solved except in special circumstances, e.g., periodic disturbances (spin waves).
summary:
Title: New Insights on "Double Exchange" Suggest Zero High-Temperature Curie-Weiss Constant

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review, physicists Philip W. Anderson and Hiroshi Hasegawa challenge the traditional understanding of double exchange, a crucial interaction between magnetic ions primarily employed in the high-temperature expansion of the susceptibility. The researchers propose that the high-temperature Curie-Weiss constant should ideally be zero, contradicting the observed behavior in manganites where double exchange is presumed to play a significant role.

The newly proposed findings suggest that the average energy for states of large total spin equals that for low-spin states, a counterintuitive result that could potentially revise our current understanding of these interactions. The scientists support their claims with calculations for a pair of ions, considering general spin $S$ and transfer integral, $b$, and internal exchange integral, $J$. This study paves the way for further investigations into the behavior of spin systems in semiclassical physics.

title: Electroluminescence of doped organic thin films
abstract: Electroluminescent (EL) devices are constructed using multilayer organic thin films. The basic structure consists of a hole-transport layer and a luminescent layer. The hole-transport layer is an amorphous diamine film in which the only mobile carrier is the hole. The luminescent layer consists of a host material, 8-hydroxyquinoline aluminum (Alq), which predominantly transports electrons. High radiance has been achieved at an operating voltage of less than 10 V. By doping the Alq layer with highly fluorescent molecules, the EL efficiency has been improved by about a factor of 2 in comparison with the undoped cell. Representative dopants are coumarins and DCMs. The EL quantum efficiency of the doped system is about 2.5%, photon/electron. The EL colors can be readily tuned from the blue-green to orange-red by a suitable choice of dopants as well as by changing the concentration of the dopant. In the doped system the electron-hole recombination and emission zones can be confined to about 50 Å near the hole-transport interface. In the undoped Alq, the EL emission zone is considerably larger due to exciton diffusion. The multilayer doped EL structure offers a simple means for the direct determination of exciton diffusion length.
summary:
Title: "New Developments in Organic Lighting: Scientists Improve Electroluminescence Efficiency"

Summary:
A team of researchers led by Chak Wah Tang, S. A. VanSlyke, and C. H. Chen have made significant strides in the field of materials science with a new approach to electroluminescent (EL) devices. The scientists have created EL devices utilizing multilayer organic thin films, which consist of a hole-transport layer and a luminescent layer. By doping the central luminescent layer with highly fluorescent molecules such as coumarins and DCMs, the researchers have managed to improve the efficiency of electroluminescence by a factor of two compared to undoped cells. This discovery not only offers exciting prospects for future applications in organic electronics but also allows for tuning the EL colors from blue-green to orange-red. The study published in the Journal of Applied Physics, sheds light on the direct determination of exciton diffusion length within these multilayer doped structures.

title: Contact Electron-Spin Coupling of Nuclear Magnetic Moments
abstract: The valence-bond theory for the contact electron-spin coupling of nuclear magnetic moments is used to calculate the proton-proton, proton-fluorine, and fluorine-fluorine coupling constants in ethanic and ethylenic molecules. A considerable simplification is introduced into the theory by approximations which reduce the problem to one involving only a small number of electrons and canonical structures. The agreement between calculated and experimental values is such as to demonstrate that the mechanism considered is the one of primary importance for the nuclear coupling in the compounds studied. Of particular interest is the theoretical confirmation of the observation that in ethylenic compounds the trans coupling between nuclei (HH, HF, FF) is considerably larger than cis coupling.
summary:
Chemistry Study Confirms Key Mechanism in Nuclear Interactions

Nobel laureate Martin Karplus' research published in The Journal of Chemical Physics sheds light on the contact electron-spin coupling of nuclear magnetic moments, focusing on fluorine and protons. The study uses the valence-bond theory to calculate coupling constants in ethanol and ethylene compounds.

By simplifying the theory through select approximations that consider a minimal number of electrons and canonical structures, Karplus' work demonstrates that this mechanism is significant for nuclear couplings in the studied compounds. Notably, the research provides theoretical support for the observation that interactions between nuclei (HH, HF, FF) in ethylenic compounds are stronger in a trans configuration compared to cis.

title: Behavior of the Electronic Dielectric Constant in Covalent and Ionic Materials
abstract: Refractive-index dispersion data below the interband absorption edge in more than 100 widely different solids and liquids are analyzed using a single-effective-oscillator fit of the form ${n}^{2}\ensuremath{-}1=\frac{{E}_{d}{E}_{0}}{({E}_{0}^{2}\ensuremath{-}{\ensuremath{\hbar}}^{2}{\ensuremath{\omega}}^{2})}$, where $\ensuremath{\hbar}\ensuremath{\omega}$ is the photon energy, ${E}_{0}$ is the single oscillator energy, and ${E}_{d}$ is the dispersion energy. The parameter ${E}_{d}$, which is a measure of the strength of interband optical transitions, is found to obey the simple empirical relationship ${E}_{d}=\ensuremath{\beta}{N}_{c}{Z}_{a}{N}_{e}$, where ${N}_{c}$ is the coordination number of the cation nearest neighbor to the anion, ${Z}_{a}$ is the formal chemical valency of the anion, ${N}_{e}$ is the effective number of valence electrons per anion (usually ${N}_{e}=8$), and $\ensuremath{\beta}$ is essentially two-valued, taking on the "ionic" value ${\ensuremath{\beta}}_{i}=0.26\ifmmode\pm\else\textpm\fi{}0.04$ eV for halides and most oxides, and the "covalent" value ${\ensuremath{\beta}}_{c}=0.37\ifmmode\pm\else\textpm\fi{}0.05$ eV for the tetrahedrally bonded ${A}^{N}{B}^{8\ensuremath{-}N}$ zinc-blende- and diamond-type structures, as well as for scheelite-structure oxides and some iodates and carbonates. Wurtzite-structure crystals form a transitional group between ionic and covalent crystal classes. Experimentally, it is also found that ${E}_{d}$ does not depend significantly on either the bandgap or the volume density of valence electrons. The experimental results are related to the fundamental ${\ensuremath{\epsilon}}_{2}$ spectrum via appropriately defined moment integrals. It is found, using relationships between moment integrals, that for a particularly simple choice of a model ${\ensuremath{\epsilon}}_{2}$ spectrum, viz., constant optical-frequency conductivity with high- and low-frequency cutoffs, the bandgap parameter ${E}_{a}$ in the high-frequency sum rule introduced by Hopfield provides the connection between the single-oscillator parameters (${E}_{0},{E}_{d}$) and the Phillips static-dielectric-constant parameters (${E}_{g},\ensuremath{\hbar}{\ensuremath{\omega}}_{p}$), i.e., ${(\ensuremath{\hbar}{\ensuremath{\omega}}_{p})}^{2}={E}_{a}{E}_{d} \mathrm{and} {E}_{g}^{2}={E}_{a}{E}_{0}$. Finally, it is suggested that the observed dependence of ${E}_{d}$ on coordination number and valency implies that an understanding of refractive-index behavior may lie in a localized molecular theory of optical transitions.
summary:
Scientists S. H. Wemple and M. DiDomenico explore the behavior of electronic dielectric constant in various materials, including ionic and covalent compounds, in a study published in Physical review. B, Solid state.

The research shows that interband optical transitions strength, represented by the parameter ${E}_{d}$, can be quantified using a simple empirical formula that takes into account the coordination number, chemical valency, and effective number of valence electrons per anion. The findings suggest two distinct behavior patterns for ionic (halides and most oxides) and covalent compounds (zinc-blende-, diamond-type structures and some other specific oxides, iodates, and carbonates).

The researchers believe that this observed dependence of ${E}_{d}$ on coordination number and valency could indicate a localized molecular theory as the key to understanding refractive-index behavior in these materials. The study aims to advance our understanding of the fundamental physics and properties within ionic and covalent structures.

title: Entropy-stabilized oxides
abstract: Abstract Configurational disorder can be compositionally engineered into mixed oxide by populating a single sublattice with many distinct cations. The formulations promote novel and entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter where metal cations are incorporated in new ways. Here, through rigorous experiments, a simple thermodynamic model, and a five-component oxide formulation, we demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state. In the latter, cation distributions are proven to be random and homogeneous. The findings validate the hypothesis that deliberate configurational disorder provides an orthogonal strategy to imagine and discover new phases of crystalline matter and untapped opportunities for property engineering.
summary:
Title: New Class of Entropy-Stabilized Oxides Discovered

In a groundbreaking study published in Nature Communications, researchers led by Christina M. Rost have unveiled a novel class of oxides. These unique oxides, produced through the introduction of compositional disorder into their structure, offer new and stable forms of crystalline matter.

By strategically populating a single sublattice with multiple distinct cations, the team has engineered mixed oxides that incorporate metals into new configurations. This work not only validates the hypothesis but also opens up novel opportunities for property engineering. The study suggests that entropy, a measure of disorder or randomness in a system, plays a dominant role in shaping the thermodynamic landscape of these materials, driving reversible solid-state transformations between multi-phase and single-phase states. The findings emphasize configurational disorder as an effective strategy for discovering new phases of crystalline matter.

title: Moiré bands in twisted double-layer graphene
abstract: A moiré pattern is formed when two copies of a periodic pattern are overlaid with a relative twist. We address the electronic structure of a twisted two-layer graphene system, showing that in its continuum Dirac model the moiré pattern periodicity leads to moiré Bloch bands. The two layers become more strongly coupled and the Dirac velocity crosses zero several times as the twist angle is reduced. For a discrete set of magic angles the velocity vanishes, the lowest moiré band flattens, and the Dirac-point density-of-states and the counterflow conductivity are strongly enhanced.
summary: Researchers Rafi Bistritzer and A.H. MacDonald, in a new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, delve into the intriguing world of twisted double-layer graphene. The scientists focus on the Moiré pattern that arises when two periodic patterns with a degree of twist overlap. In this research, they reveal how the Moiré pattern affects the electronic structure in the system's continuum Dirac model, resulting in what they call "Moiré Bloch bands." As the twist angle lessens, the layers grow more interconnected, and the Dirac velocity crosses zero multiple times. For specific "magic angles," the velocity vanishes completely, leading to the flattening of the lowest Moiré band, and a significant enhancement in the Dirac-point density-of-states and counterflow conductivity. This work adds to the expanding field of condensed matter physics, highlighting the potential for further advancements in understanding and harnessing twist-induced phenomena in bilayer graphene.

title: New material for permanent magnets on a base of Nd and Fe (invited)
abstract: A new compound composed of Nd, Fe, and a small quantity of B (about 1 wt. %) has been found, which has a tetragonal structure with lattice constants a=0.880 nm and c=1.221 nm. This phase, which has the approximate composition, 12 at. % Nd, 6 at. % B and balance Fe, possesses remarkable magnetic properties. From the approach to saturation an anisotroy constant of about 3.5 MJ/m3 can be calculated, while saturation magnetization amounts to 1.35 T. The magnetization versus temperature curve shows a Curie temperature of 585 K, which is much higher than those of the Fe and light rare earth binary compounds. Based on the new compound, sintered permanent magnets have been developed which have a record high energy product. Permanent magnet properties and physical properties of a typical specimen which has the composition Nd15B8Fe77 are as follows: Br =1.23 T, HcB =880 kA/m, HcI =960 kA/m, (BH)max =290 kJ/m3, temperature coefficient of Br =−1260 ppm/K, density=7.4 Mg/m3, specific resistivity=1.4 μΩm, Vickers hardness=600, flexual strength=250 MPa.

title: Superconductivity at 38 K in the Iron Arsenide<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mi>Ba</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">K</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mi>Fe</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mi>As</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:math>
abstract: The ternary iron arsenide BaFe2As2 becomes superconducting by hole doping, which was achieved by partial substitution of the barium site with potassium. We have discovered bulk superconductivity at T{c}=38 K in (Ba1-xKx)Fe2As2 with x approximately 0.4. The parent compound BaFe2As2 crystallizes in the tetragonal ThCr2Si2-type structure, which consists of (FeAs);{delta-} iron arsenide layers separated by Ba2+ ions. BaFe2As2 is a poor metal and exhibits a spin density wave anomaly at 140 K. By substituting Ba2+ for K+ ions we have introduced holes in the (FeAs);{-} layers, which suppress the anomaly and induce superconductivity. The T{c} of 38 K in (Ba0.6K0.4)Fe2As2 is the highest in hole doped iron arsenide superconductors so far. Therefore, we were able to expand this class of superconductors by oxygen-free compounds with the ThCr2Si2-type structure.
summary:
Title: Breakthrough Discovery Boosts Superconductivity in Iron Arsenide Compounds

New research published in Physical Review Letters has opened a door for expanding the class of iron arsenide superconductors without the need for oxygen, reaching a record high temperature of 38 Kelvin. The study, led by scientists Marcus Tegel, M. Rotter and Dirk Johrendt, focused on the ternary compound BaFe2As2, achieving superconductivity by hole doping through partial substitution of barium with potassium. The researchers found that a composition of (Ba0.6K0.4)Fe2As2 suppressed an anomaly present in the parent compound BaFe2As2 and induced superconductivity, making this the highest temperature reported for hole-doped iron arsenide superconductors to date. This groundbreaking work could pave the way for further research into these superconductor materials.

title: The physics of simple metal clusters: experimental aspects and simple models
abstract: The study of simple metal clusters has burgeoned in the last decade, motivated by the growing interest in the evolution of physical properties from the atom to the bulk solid, a progression passing through the domain of atomic clusters. On the experimental side, the rapid development of new techniques for producing the clusters and for probing and detecting them has resulted in a phenomenal increase in our knowledge of these systems. For clusters of the simplest metals, the alkali and noble metals, the electronic structure is dominated by the number of valence electrons, and the ionic cores are of secondary importance. These electrons are delocalized, and the electronic system exhibits a shell structure that is closely related to the well-known nuclear shell structure. In this article the results from a broad range of experiments are reviewed and compared with theory. Included are the behavior of the mass-abundance spectra, polarizabilities, ionization potentials, photoelectron spectra, optical spectra, and fragmentation phenomena.
summary:
Title: "New Review Explores Delocalized Electrons in Simple Metal Clusters"

In a comprehensive review published in Reviews of Modern Physics, Walt A. de Heer delves into the burgeoning field of simple metal clusters. The study explores the evolution of physical properties from individual atoms to bulk solids, highlighting the essential role of delocalized electrons in the atomic cluster domain.

The article focuses on alkali and noble metals, where valence electrons dominate electronic structure, while ionic cores play a secondary role. Experimental data on mass-abundance spectra, polarizabilities, ionization potentials, photoelectron spectra, optical spectra, and fragmentation phenomena are reviewed in comparison to theoretical models. This work aims to further our understanding of these systems, paving the way for future advancements in the field of physics.

title: Landauer formula for the current through an interacting electron region
abstract: A Landauer formula for the current through a region of interacting electrons is derived using the nonequilibrium Keldysh formalism. The case of proportionate coupling to the left and right leads, where the formula takes an especially simple form, is studied in more detail. Two particular examples where interactions give rise to novel effects in the current are discussed: In the Kondo regime, an enhanced conductance is predicted, while a suppressed conductance is predicted for tunneling through a quantum dot in the fractional quantum Hall regime.
summary:
Title: Breakthrough in Quantum Electronics: New Landauer Formula for Interacting Electrons Unveiled

Physicists Yigal Meir and Ned S. Wingreen, writing in Physical Review Letters, have derived a new Landauer formula for the current through regions of interacting electrons. This groundbreaking discovery utilizes the nonequilibrium Keldysh formalism and presents a simplified form for cases where coupling to left and right leads is proportionate.

Meir and Wingreen's work highlights two significant examples: in the Kondo regime, enhanced conductance is predicted due to electron interactions; while tunneling through a quantum dot in the fractional quantum Hall regime shows a suppressed conductance. This research promises to advance our understanding of non-equilibrium thermodynamics within quantum systems and could lead to novel developments in quantum technologies.

title: Four-Terminal Phase-Coherent Conductance
abstract: A conductance formula for a sample of arbitrary shape with four terminals is derived to describe transport in the limit where carriers can traverse the sample without suffering phase-destroying events. The Onsager-Casimir symmetry relations are deduced. Experiments measure an off-diagonal Onsager coefficient and the magnetoconductance of such a sample is asymmetric even in the presence of an Aharonov-Bohm flux only. Symmetry relations between conductance measurements which exchange the role of current and voltage leads are predicted.
summary:
### Physicist Proposes Groundbreaking Formula for Four-Terminal Conductance

In a landmark paper published in Physical Review Letters, Swiss physicist M. Büttiker has derived a formula to describe transport in four-terminal conductors, where particles can seamlessly traverse the sample without undergoing phase-destructive events. The paper builds upon the foundational Onsager-Casimir symmetry relations and offers new insights into the behavior of asymmetric magnetoconductance and off-diagonal Onsager coefficients in the presence of an Aharonov-Bohm flux. The work, significant for its potential to reshape our understanding of conductance in condensed matter physics and geometry symmetry, could pave the way for future experiments and applications.

title: Intrinsic and extrinsic performance limits of graphene devices on SiO2.
abstract: The linear dispersion relation in graphene gives rise to a surprising prediction: the resistivity due to isotropic scatterers, such as white-noise disorder or phonons, is independent of carrier density, n. Here we show that electron-acoustic phonon scattering is indeed independent of n, and contributes only 30 Omega to graphene's room-temperature resistivity. At a technologically relevant carrier density of 1 x1012 cm-2, we infer a mean free path for electron-acoustic phonon scattering of >2 microm and an intrinsic mobility limit of 2 x 105 cm2 V-1 s-1. If realized, this mobility would exceed that of InSb, the inorganic semiconductor with the highest known mobility ( approximately 7.7 x 104 cm2 V-1 s-1; ref. 9) and that of semiconducting carbon nanotubes ( approximately 1 x 105 cm2 V-1 s-1; ref. 10). A strongly temperature-dependent resistivity contribution is observed above approximately 200 K (ref. 8); its magnitude, temperature dependence and carrier-density dependence are consistent with extrinsic scattering by surface phonons at the SiO2 substrate and limit the room-temperature mobility to approximately 4 x 104 cm2 V-1 s-1, indicating the importance of substrate choice for graphene devices.
summary:
Graphene device performance study shatters expectations with intrinsic mobility potential

Graphene, a two-dimensional carbon material, has long been hailed for its exceptional properties. A recent study published in Nature Nanotechnology, led by researchers Jianhao Chen and Chaun Jang, reveals that graphene's room temperature resistivity might be surprisingly independent of carrier density due to electron-acoustic phonon scattering, making it possible to reach mobilities exceeding those of InSb – an inorganic semiconductor with the highest known mobility to date.

However, the researchers found that a temperature-dependent resistivity contribution limits graphene's room-temperature mobility to approximately 4 x 10^4 cm^2 V^-1 s^-1, highlighting the crucial role of substrate choice in optimizing graphene devices and pushing the boundaries of condensed matter physics.

title: Determination of effective permittivity and permeability of metamaterials from reflection and transmission coefficients
abstract: We analyze the reflection and transmission coefficients calculated from transfer matrix simulations on finite lenghts of electromagnetic metamaterials, to determine the effective permittivity and permeability. We perform this analysis on structures composed of periodic arrangements of wires, split ring resonators (SRRs) and both wires and SRRs. We find the recovered frequency-dependent permittivity and permeability are entirely consistent with analytic expressions predicted by effective medium arguments. Of particular relevance are that a wire medium exhibits a frequency region in which the real part of permittivity is negative, and SRRs produce a frequency region in which the real part of permeability is negative. In the combination structure, at frequencies where both the recovered real part of permittivity and permeability are simultaneously negative, the real part of the index-of-refraction is found also to be unambigously negative.
summary:
**New Study Sheds Light on Negative Permittivity and Permeability in Metamaterials**

In a groundbreaking scientific study published in Physical Review B, Condensed Matter, researchers led by David R. Smith have made strides in determining the effective permittivity and permeability of metamaterials using reflection and transmission coefficients. The findings draw from electromagnetic simulations of structures made up of wires, split-ring resonators (SRRs), and their combination.

The researchers found that the recovered frequency-dependent permittivity and permeability align with analytic expressions predicted by effective medium arguments, paving the way for a better understanding of metamaterial properties like negative refraction. This study promises to advance the field of physics and could lead to innovative applications in electromagnetics and optical engineering.

title: Multiple-scattering calculations of x-ray-absorption spectra
abstract: A high-order multiple-scattering (MS) approach to the calculation of polarized x-ray-absorption spectra, which includes both x-ray-absorption fine structure and x-ray-absorption near-edge structure, is presented. Efficient calculations in arbitrary systems are carried out by using a curved-wave MS path formalism that ignores negligible paths, and has an energy-dependent self-energy and MS Debye-Waller factors. Embedded-atom background absorption calculations on an absolute energy scale are included. The theory is illustrated for metallic Cu, Cd, and Pt. For these cases the MS expansion is found to converge to within typical experimental accuracy, both to experiment and to full MS theories (e.g., band structure), by using only a few dozen important paths, which are primarily single-scattering, focusing, linear, and triangular.
summary:
Headline:
New High-Order Scattering Method Accurately Predicts X-ray Data for Metals

Summary:
In the field of physics, researchers have developed an innovative method to calculate polarized x-ray absorption spectra with high accuracy for metals like Copper (Cu), Cadmium (Cd), and Platinum (Pt). This multiple-scattering approach includes both x-ray absorption fine structure and near-edge structure, enabling expedient calculations without compromising on precision. The technique is effective due to its curved-wave formalism that disregards insignificant paths, energy-dependent self-energy, and MS Debye-Waller factors. Moreover, embedded-atom background absorption calculations are included using an absolute energy scale. This new method converges within experimental accuracy by utilizing only a few dozen essential paths in the spectra analysis.

title: Periodic boundary conditions inab initiocalculations
abstract: The convergence of the electrostatic energy in calculations using periodic boundary conditions is considered in the context of periodic solids and localized aperiodic systems in the gas and condensed phases. Conditions for the absolute convergence of the total energy in periodic boundary conditions are obtained, and their implications for calculations of the properties of polarized solids under the zero-field assumption are discussed. For aperiodic systems the exact electrostatic energy functional in periodic boundary conditions is obtained. The convergence in such systems is considered in the limit of large supercells, where, in the gas phase, the computational effort is proportional to the volume. It is shown that for neutral localized aperiodic systems in either the gas or condensed phases, the energy can always be made to converge as O(${\mathit{L}}^{\mathrm{\ensuremath{-}}5}$) where L is the linear dimension of the supercell. For charged systems, convergence at this rate can be achieved after adding correction terms to the energy to account for spurious interactions induced by the periodic boundary conditions. These terms are derived exactly for the gas phase and heuristically for the condensed phase.
summary:
Headline:
"New Insights in Electrostatics Calculations: Periodic Boundary Conditions Optimized for Polarized Solids and Aperiodic Systems"

Summary:
A new study published in Physical Review B, Condensed Matter offers significant advancements in the field of condensed matter physics. Researchers Guy Makov and M.C. Payne focus on optimizing periodic boundary conditions for calculations involving polarized solids and aperiodic systems. The findings provide essential conditions for the absolute convergence of total energy in periodic boundary conditions, which can be particularly useful for determining properties of polarized solids under the zero-field assumption. For aperiodic systems, an exact electrostatic energy functional has been obtained, addressing concerns about system convergence in large supercells. Notably, the study reveals that energy in neutral localized aperiodic systems can always converge at O(${\mathit{L}}^{\mathrm{\ensuremath{-}}5}$) rate, offering a more efficient computational approach for these complex systems. The team also addresses spurious interactions induced by periodic boundary conditions in charged systems, providing correction terms to ensure convergence at the improved rate.

title: Two-dimensional electron gases induced by spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization charges in N- and Ga-face AlGaN/GaN heterostructures
abstract: Carrier concentration profiles of two-dimensional electron gases are investigated in wurtzite, Ga-face AlxGa1−xN/GaN/AlxGa1−xN and N-face GaN/AlxGa1−xN/GaN heterostructures used for the fabrication of field effect transistors. Analysis of the measured electron distributions in heterostructures with AlGaN barrier layers of different Al concentrations (0.15&lt;x&lt;0.5) and thickness between 20 and 65 nm demonstrate the important role of spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization on the carrier confinement at GaN/AlGaN and AlGaN/GaN interfaces. Characterization of the electrical properties of nominally undoped transistor structures reveals the presence of high sheet carrier concentrations, increasing from 6×1012 to 2×1013 cm−2 in the GaN channel with increasing Al-concentration from x=0.15 to 0.31. The observed high sheet carrier concentrations and strong confinement at specific interfaces of the N- and Ga-face pseudomorphic grown heterostructures can be explained as a consequence of interface charges induced by piezoelectric and spontaneous polarization effects.
summary:
**Breakthrough in Materials Science: Study Explores Two-dimensional Electron Gases Induced by Polarization Charges**

In a groundbreaking study presented in the Journal of Applied Physics, researchers led by O. Ambacher have shed light on the role of spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization charges in two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) induced in N- and Ga-face AlGaN/GaN heterostructures. The study aims to help improve field effect transistors used in various electronic devices.

Focusing on the pseudomorphic grown heterostructures, the researchers observed high sheet carrier concentrations increasing from 6×10^12 to 2×10^13 cm^-2 in GaN channels with Al-concentration varying from x=0.15 to 0.31 due to the presence of interface charges induced by piezoelectric and spontaneous polarization effects. This important work demonstrates the significant role of these effects for carrier confinement at critical interfaces in the GaN/AlGaN and AlGaN/GaN heterostructures, pushing the frontier of understanding and utilization of materials within semiconductor technology.

title: Nucleation and growth of thin films
abstract: A review is given of the nucleation and growth processes occurring in thin film formation. Emphasis is given to quantitative nucleation theories and to the role of electron microscopy and surface techniques in providing data to test such theories. The relations between the thermodynamics of adsorption and the kinetics of crystal growth is stressed. Experimental examples are taken from the island growth, layer plus island (or Stranski-Krastanov) and layer growth modes. The shapes of growing crystallites are briefly discussed.
summary:
Title: "A Comprehensive Review on Nucleation and Growth of Thin Films"

In a compelling new study published in Reports on Progress in Physics, researchers J. A. Venables, G. D. T. Spiller, and M. Hanbücken delve into the intricate processes governing the formation of thin films, shedding light on nucleation and growth mechanisms.

This significant work emphasizes quantitative nucleation theories and the instrumental role of electron microscopy and surface techniques in validating these theories. The researchers highlight the relationship between adsorption thermodynamics and crystal growth kinetics, drawing on examples spanning island growth, Stranski-Krastanov growth mode, and layer growth. Additionally, the paper provides insights into the shapes of developing crystallites within this context.
