title: Photoelectrolysis and physical properties of the semiconducting electrode WO2
abstract: The behavior of semiconducting electrodes for photoelectrolysis of water is examined in terms of the physical properties of the semiconductor. The semiconductor-electrolyte junction is treated as a simple Schottky barrier, and the photocurrent is described using this model. The approach is appropriate since large-band-gap semiconductors have an intrinsic oxygen overpotential which removes the electrode reaction kinetics as the rate-limiting step. The model is successful in describing the wavelength and potential dependence of the photocurrent in WO3 and allows a determination of the band gap, optical absorption depth, minority-carrier diffusion length, flat-band potential, and the nature of the fundamental optical transition (direct or indirect). It is shown for WO3 that minority-carrier diffusion plays a limited role in determining the photoresponse of the semiconductor-electrolyte junction. There are indications that the diffusion length in this low carrier mobility material is determined by diffusion-controlled bulk recombination processes rather than the more common trap-limited recombination. It is also shown that the fundamental optical transition is indirect and that the band-gap energy depends relatively strongly on applied potential and electrolyte. This effect seems to be the result of field-induced crystallographic distortions in antiferroelectric WO3.
summary:
Study offers insights into semiconductor's role in water photoelectrolysis

A new study by M. A. Butler published in the Journal of Applied Physics provides valuable insights into the physical properties of semiconducting electrodes crucial for the photoelectrolysis of water. The research focuses on WO3, a large-band-gap semiconductor with an intrinsic oxygen overpotential that significantly expedites the process by eliminating electrode reaction kinetics as the rate-limiting step.

Butler's approach uses a Schottky barrier model to describe the behavior at the semiconductor-electrolyte junction and predict the wavelength and potential dependence of the photocurrent. Findings reveal that minority-carrier diffusion plays a minimal role in determining the photoresponse of the semiconductor-electrolyte junction for WO3.

Additionally, the research indicates that the fundamental optical transition in WO3 is indirect and that the band-gap energy varies relatively strongly with applied potential and electrolyte. This result seems to be due to field-induced crystallographic distortions in antiferroelectric WO3. The findings offer new perspectives on optimizing materials for photoelectrolysis applications by better understanding the role of semiconductors and their electrolytes.

title: Renormalization, vortices, and symmetry-breaking perturbations in the two-dimensional planar model
abstract: The classical planar Heisenberg model is studied at low temperatures by means of renormalization theory and a series of exact transformations. A numerical study of the Migdal recursion relation suggests that models with short-range isotropic interactions rapidly become equivalent to a simplified model system proposed by Villain. A series of exact transformations then allows us to treat the Villain model analytically at low temperatures. To lowest order in a parameter which becomes exponentially small with decreasing temperature, we reproduce results obtained previously by Kosterlitz. We also examine the effect of symmetry-breaking crystalline fields on the isotropic planar model. A numerical study of the Migdal recursion scheme suggests that these fields (which must occur in real quasi-two-dimensional crystals) are strongly relevant variables, leading to critical behavior distinct from that found for the planar model. However, a more exact low-temperature treatment of the Villain model shows that hexagonal crystalline fields eventually become irrelevant at temperatures below the ${T}_{c}$ of the isotropic model. Isotropic planar critical behavior should be experimentally accessible in this case. Nonuniversal behavior may result if cubic crystalline fields dominate the symmetry breaking. Interesting duality transformations, which aid in the analysis of symmetry-breaking fields are also discussed.
summary:
Scientific Paper Finds Renormalization Theory Useful for Studying Two-Dimensional Planar Models

Physical Review B: Solid State published a revealing paper, co-authored by Jorge V. José and others, proposing that low-temperature behavior of the classical planar Heisenberg model can be analyzed using renormalization theory. The study suggests that short-range isotropic interactions in models quickly align with simplified models by Villain.

The authors successfully apply a series of refined analytical techniques to understand the impact of symmetry-breaking crystalline fields on the isotropic planar model. While such fields are essential in quasi-two-dimensional crystals, their critical behavior seems distinct from that of the plain planar model. However, at temperatures below the critical point Tc of the isotropic model, hexagonal crystalline fields reportedly lose relevance, suggesting possible experimental accessibility for isotropic planar critical behavior. Researchers also found intriguing duality transformations beneficial in analyzing symmetry-breaking phenomena.

title: The Dielectric Polarization of Polar Liquids
abstract: An extension of the Onsager theory of dielectric polarization is presented. The local dielectric constant is approximated by the macroscopic dielectric constant of the fluid in a region outside a molecule and its first shell of neighbors rather than in the entire region exterior to the molecule. In addition to the molecular dipole moment, the average value 〈cosγ〉Av of the cosine of the angle between neighbor dipoles is a determining factor. Hindered relative rotation of neighboring molecules produces a correlation between their orientations and prevents 〈cosγ〉Av from vanishing. The theory is applied to liquid water under the assumption of tetrahedral coordination and directed bonds between neighboring molecules.
summary: In a groundbreaking study published in "The Journal of Chemical Physics," physicist John G. Kirkwood presents an extension to the Onsager dielectric polarization theory. The work focuses on polar liquids, particularly liquid water, where Kirkwood approximates the local dielectric constant using the macroscopic value of adjacent molecules and their neighbors. This new approach incorporates the average cosine of angles between neighbor dipoles (〈cosγ〉Av) in addition to the molecular dipole moment. Notably, the theory takes into account hindered relative rotation of nearby molecules to explain the orientation correlation and prevent 〈cosγ〉Av from becoming negligible. This exciting research holds potential for advancing our understanding of chemical polarity and polarization in electrochemistry, particularly in studies of water structures and molecular interactions.

title: Percolation and cluster distribution. I. Cluster multiple labeling technique and critical concentration algorithm
abstract: A new approach for the determination of the critical percolation concentration, percolation probabilities, and cluster size distributions is presented for the site percolation problem. The novel "cluster multiple labeling technique" is described for both two- and three-dimensional crystal structures. Its distinctive feature is the assignment of alternate labels to sites belonging to the same cluster. These sites are members of a simulated finite random lattice. An algorithm useful for the determination of the critical percolation concentration of a finite lattice is also presented. This algorithm is especially useful when applied in conjunction with the cluster multiple labeling technique. The basic features of this technique are illustrated by applying it to a small planar square lattice. Numerical results are given for a triangular subcrystal containing up to 9 000 000 sites. These results compare favorably with the exact value of the infinite lattice critical percolation concentration.
summary:
Study proposes new method for determining critical percolation concentrations and cluster size distributions

title: Time-dependent transport in interacting and noninteracting resonant-tunneling systems
abstract:
We consider a mesoscopic region coupled to two leads under the influence of
external time-dependent voltages. The time dependence is coupled to source and
drain contacts, the gates controlling the tunnel- barrier heights, or to the
gates which define the mesoscopic region. We derive, with the Keldysh
nonequilibrium Green function technique, a formal expression for the fully
nonlinear, time-dependent current through the system. The analysis admits
arbitrary interactions in the mesoscopic region, but the leads are treated as
noninteracting. For proportionate coupling to the leads, the time-averaged
current is simply the integral between the chemical potentials of the
time-averaged density of states, weighted by the coupling to the leads, in
close analogy to the time-independent result of Meir and Wingreen (PRL {\bf
68}, 2512 (1992)). Analytical and numerical results for the exactly solvable
non-interacting resonant-tunneling system are presented.
summary:
Title: New Study Unveils Time-Dependent Transport in Quantum Tunneling Systems

Subheading: Researchers propose a groundbreaking formula to analyze the nonlinear, time-dependent current flow in complex quantum systems.

Article:

In a breakthrough advancement within the realm of mesoscopic physics, researchers have made significant strides in understanding how external time-dependent voltages affect quantum tunneling in small conductors. Led by Antti-Pekka Jauho, Ned S. Wingreen, and Yigal Meir, this new research unveils a formal expression for the nonlinear, time-dependent current flowing through such systems.

Previous work by Meir and Wingreen (Physical Review Letters, 1992) laid the foundation for understanding how these systems behave without external time dependencies. Now, the team's latest endeavor seeks to expand upon that research by incorporating complex scenarios involving coupled time-dependent voltages, gate controls, and interactions within the mesoscopic region while treating the leads as noninteracting.

The results provide an analytical formula that calculates the averaged current flowing through the system, bridging the gap between time-independent and nonlinear, time-dependent phenomena in quantum tunneling systems. Notably, the research presents numerical and analytical results for exactly solvable non-interacting resonant-tunneling systems, opening up new possibilities for investigating and harnessing these fascinating properties in real-world applications.

title: Hopping Conductivity in Disordered Systems
abstract: By considering a model in which charge is transported via phonon-induced tunneling of electrons between localized states which are randomly distributed in energy and position, Mott has obtained an electrical conductivity of the form $\ensuremath{\sigma}\ensuremath{\propto}\mathrm{exp}[\ensuremath{-}{(\frac{\ensuremath{\lambda}{\ensuremath{\alpha}}^{3}}{{\ensuremath{\rho}}_{0}\mathrm{kT}})}^{\frac{1}{4}}]$. Here $T$ is the temperature of the system, ${\ensuremath{\rho}}_{0}$ is the density of states at the Fermi level, $\ensuremath{\lambda}$ is a dimensionless constant, and ${\ensuremath{\alpha}}^{\ensuremath{-}1}$ is the distance for exponential decay of the wave functions. We rederive these results, relating $\ensuremath{\lambda}$ to the critical density of a certain dimensionless percolation problem, and we estimate $\ensuremath{\lambda}$ to be approximately 16. The applicability of the model to experimental observations on amorphous Ge, Si, and C is discussed.
summary:
Article Title: A New Insight into Electrical Conductivity in Disordered Systems

In a groundbreaking study by Vinay Ambegaokar, B. I. Halperin, and J. S. Langer published in Physical Review B, the researchers presented an innovative model for hopping conductivity in disordered systems. The model considers the transport of charge via phonon-induced tunneling between localized states that are randomly distributed in energy and position.

The study, which builds upon Mott's work, yields an electrical conductivity formula of $\ensuremath{\sigma}\ensuremath{\propto}\mathrm{exp}[\ensuremath{-}{(\frac{\ensuremath{\lambda}{\ensuremath{\alpha}}^{3}}{{\ensuremath{\rho}}_{0}\mathrm{kT}})}^{\frac{1}{4}}]$. The dimensionless quantity $\ensuremath{\lambda}$ is related to the critical density of a specific percolation problem, with an estimated value of approximately 16.

The applicability of this model to experimental observations in amorphous Ge, Si, and C is discussed, potentially paving the way for a better understanding and manipulation of conductivity properties in disordered systems.

title: Generic New Platform for Topological Quantum Computation Using Semiconductor Heterostructures
abstract: We show that a film of a semiconductor in which s-wave superconductivity and Zeeman splitting are induced by the proximity effect, supports zero-energy Majorana fermion modes in the ordinary vortex excitations. Since time-reversal symmetry is explicitly broken, the edge of the film constitutes a chiral Majorana wire. The heterostructure we propose-a semiconducting thin film sandwiched between an s-wave superconductor and a magnetic insulator-is a generic system which can be used as the platform for topological quantum computation by virtue of the existence of non-Abelian Majorana fermions.
summary: In a groundbreaking discovery, scientists have developed a new platform for topological quantum computing, utilizing semiconductor heterostructures. This innovative approach builds upon the renowned Majorana concept, a theoretical particle that has been a cornerstone of quantum physics. By inducing s-wave superconductivity and Zeeman splitting in a film of a semiconductor, the researchers discovered zero-energy Majorana fermion modes in ordinary vortex excitations. This breakthrough paves the way for topological quantum computation due to the presence of non-Abelian Majorana fermions at the edge of the film, effectively creating a chiral Majorana wire. The study was published in Physical Review Letters by authors Jay D. Sau, Roman M. Lutchyn, Sumanta Tewari, and S. Das Sarma.

title: The Electrical Resistance of Binary Metallic Mixtures
abstract: The existing theories of the resistivity of mixtures assume regular arrangements of the two components, rather than random mixtures. A theory for a random mixture is given, based on the assumption that each crystal acts as if surrounded by a homogeneous medium whose properties are those of the mixture. Comparisons with experiment are made. The experimental data that have been examined fall roughly into two classes. One class consists of mixtures, where the variation of resistivity with composition disagrees violently with this theory, making it clear that the assumptions made are completely inapplicable. The remaining class consists of mixtures which generally agree well with the theory.
summary:
Title: "New Theory Offers Insight into Electrical Conductivity of Random Metal Mixtures"

Authors Rolf Landauer present a groundbreaking theory in the Journal of Applied Physics, challenging conventional understandings about the electrical resistance of binary metallic mixtures. Unlike existing theories that focus on regular arrangements, this new approach considers random mixtures, a scenario not previously addressed. The new strategy assumes each crystal interacts with a homogeneous medium mirroring the mixture's properties. Initial comparisons with experimental data reveal two categories: mixtures where resistivity disagreements highlight the theory's inapplicability, and those generally aligning well with the proposed theory.

title: Enhanced Gilbert Damping in Thin Ferromagnetic Films
abstract: The precession of the magnetization of a ferromagnet is shown to transfer spins into adjacent normal metal layers. This "pumping" of spins slows down the precession corresponding to an enhanced Gilbert damping constant in the Landau-Lifshitz equation. The damping is expressed in terms of the scattering matrix of the ferromagnetic layer, which is accessible to model and first-principles calculations. Our estimates for permalloy thin films explain the trends observed in recent experiments.
summary:
Title: Breakthrough in Magnetism Research: Scientists Discover Method to Boost Spin Damping in Thin Metallic Films

New research published in Physical Review Letters has unveiled a fascinating new phenomenon wherein magnetization precession in ferromagnetic films can transfer spins into adjacent normal metal layers. This unprecedented finding, referred to as spin pumping, slows down the precession and leads to a heightened Gilbert damping constant in the Landau-Lifshitz equation—a critical mathematical model in condensed matter physics.

The study, led by Yaroslav Tserkovnyak, Arne Brataas, and G. Bauer, focused on Permalloy—a type of ferromagnetic metal—and offers estimates that accurately explain trends observed in recent experiments in the field. This new discovery may unlock potential applications for advanced magnetic technologies based on spin effects.

title: Crystal structures and elastic properties of superhard<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ir</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">N</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>and<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ir</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">N</mml:mi><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>from first principles
abstract: First principles calculations were performed to investigate the structural, elastic, and electronic properties of $\mathrm{Ir}{\mathrm{N}}_{2}$ for various space groups: cubic $Fm\text{\ensuremath{-}}3m$ and $Pa\text{\ensuremath{-}}3$, hexagonal $P{3}_{2}21$, tetragonal $P{4}_{2}∕mnm$, orthorhombic $Pmmn$, $Pnnm$, and $Pnn2$, and monoclinic $P{2}_{1}∕c$. Our calculation indicates that the $P{2}_{1}∕c$ phase with arsenopyrite-type structure is energetically more stable than the other phases. It is semiconducting (the remaining phases are metallic) and contains diatomic N-N with the bond distance of $1.414\phantom{\rule{0.3em}{0ex}}\mathrm{\AA{}}$. These characters are consistent with the experimental facts that $\mathrm{Ir}{\mathrm{N}}_{2}$ is in lower symmetry and nonmetallic. Our conclusion is also in agreement with the recent theoretical studies that the most stable phase of $\mathrm{Ir}{\mathrm{N}}_{2}$ is monoclinic $P{2}_{1}∕c$. The calculated bulk modulus of $373\phantom{\rule{0.3em}{0ex}}\mathrm{GPa}$ is also the highest among the considered space groups. It matches the recent theoretical values of $357\phantom{\rule{0.3em}{0ex}}\mathrm{GPa}$ within 4.3% and of $402\phantom{\rule{0.3em}{0ex}}\mathrm{GPa}$ within 7.8%, but smaller than the experimental value of $428\phantom{\rule{0.3em}{0ex}}\mathrm{GPa}$ by 14.7%. Chemical bonding and potential displacive phase transitions are discussed for $\mathrm{Ir}{\mathrm{N}}_{2}$. For $\mathrm{Ir}{\mathrm{N}}_{3}$, cubic skutterudite structure $(Im\text{\ensuremath{-}}3)$ was assumed. Our calculation indicated that it is also promising to be superhard due to the large bulk modulus of $358\phantom{\rule{0.3em}{0ex}}\mathrm{GPa}$ and shear modulus of $246\phantom{\rule{0.3em}{0ex}}\mathrm{GPa}$. The diatomic N-N bond distance is even shorter $(1.272\phantom{\rule{0.3em}{0ex}}\mathrm{\AA{}})$.
summary: Researchers Zhijian Wu and colleagues have made a breakthrough in the study of superhard compounds, with their new findings on IrN2 and IrN3 published in Physical Review B. The team's first-principles calculations reveal that the monoclinic structure (IrN2) is the most stable phase and semiconducting, characterized by diatomic N-N bonds. This finding aligns with previous theoretical studies and supports the notion that IrN2 could potentially be a superhard material. Moreover, their results suggest that IrN3 could also possess superhard properties due to its large bulk modulus and short N-N bond distance. The team is now discussing chemical bonding and potential displacive phase transitions for these promising compounds.

abstract: Heat Flow in Graphene Unsupported graphene sheets show exceptional thermal transport properties, but are these properties maintained when a graphene sheet is in contact with a substrate? Seol et al. (p. 213 ; see the Perspective by Prasher ) measured the thermal conductivity of graphene supported on silicon dioxide and found that, while the conductivity was considerably lower than that of free-standing graphene, it was still greater than that of metals such as copper. The discovery is attributed to out-of-plane flexing vibrations of the graphene playing a significant role in heat conduction, which could potentially aid in applications such as dissipating heat away from electronic circuits. This study builds upon existing research by exploring how the properties of graphene are influenced when in contact with a substrate.

abstract: Using thin film pillars approximately 100 nm in diameter, containing two Co layers of different thicknesses separated by a Cu spacer, we examine the process by which the scattering from the ferromagnetic layers of spin-polarized currents flowing perpendicular to the layers causes controlled reversal of the moment direction in the thin Co layer. The well-defined geometry permits a quantitative analysis of this spin-transfer effect, allowing tests of competing theories for the mechanism and also new insight concerning magnetic damping. When large magnetic fields are applied, the spin-polarized current no longer fully reverses the magnetic moment, but instead stimulates spin-wave excitations.

title: Novel Electronic and Magnetic Properties of Two‐Dimensional Transition Metal Carbides and Nitrides
abstract: Abstract Layered MAX phases are exfoliated into 2D single layers and multilayers, so‐called MXenes. Using first‐principles calculations, the formation and electronic properties of various MXene systems, M 2 C (M = Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Zr, Nb, Ta) and M 2 N (M = Ti, Cr, Zr) with surfaces chemically functionalized by F, OH, and O groups, are examined. Upon appropriate surface functionalization, Sc 2 C, Ti 2 C, Zr 2 C, and Hf 2 C MXenes are expected to become semiconductors. It is also derived theoretically that functionalized Cr 2 C and Cr 2 N MXenes are magnetic. Thermoelectric calculations based on the Boltzmann theory imply that semiconducting MXenes attain very large Seebeck coefficients at low temperatures.

Furthermore, the study anticipates significant thermoelectric potential for these semiconducting MXenes at low temperatures due to large Seebeck coefficients. This work not only expands our understanding of MXenes but also opens new avenues for their application in materials science and electronics.

abstract: We report strong, anisotropic magnetic relaxation of the field-cooled and zero-field-cooled magnetization along the principal axes of an Y-Ba-Cu-O single crystal and interpret it with a thermally activated flux-creep model. In the journal Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Y. Yeshurun and A. P. Malozemoff have presented a groundbreaking study on the behavior of Y-Ba-Cu-O crystals, a common superconducting material. The study, titled "Giant Flux Creep and Irreversibility in an Y-Ba-Cu-O Crystal: An Alternative to the Superconducting-Glass Model," explores the mysterious phenomenon of creep, a concept in materials science that describes deformations within crystals over time.

This breakthrough offers new directions for understanding and manipulating superconducting materials, with potential implications for applications ranging from electronics to quantum computing.

title: Ionicity of the Chemical Bond in Crystals
abstract: The nature of the chemical bond in crystals is discussed. The general theories of L. Pauling based on thermochemical data and of C. A. Coulson based on valence bond concepts are compared with a recent spectroscopic theory. Particular emphasis is placed on binary crystals of formula ${\mathrm{A}}^{N}{\mathrm{B}}^{8\ensuremath{-}N}$ which includes most tetrahedrally coordinated semiconductors as well as crystals of the rocksalt (NaCl) family. A wide range of physical properties is discussed, including crystal structure, energy bands, elastic constants, ionization energies, and impurity states. The role of quantum-mechanical sum rules and spectral moments in constructing simplified models of bond and band behavior is explored. Stress is laid throughout on methods for incorporating quantum-mechanical effects into properties of chemical bonds through algebraic relations rather than through variational solutions of the wave equation.

Title: Revisiting the Chemical Bond in Crystals: A New Perspective

In a groundbreaking review published by Reviews of Modern Physics, Dr. J. C. Phillips delves into a new interpretation of the chemical bond in crystals. The work builds upon prior research by L. Pauling and C. A. Coulson, particularly their thermochemical data and valence bond concepts, but introduces a fresh spectroscopic theory.

Phillips' review focuses on binary crystals, including tetrahedrally coordinated semiconductors and those of the rock salt (NaCl) family. Discussions range from crystal structure, energy bands, elastic constants, ionization energies to impurity states, exploring how these properties are influenced by the quantum-mechanical nature of chemical bonds.

The paper emphasizes simplified models for bond and band behavior, utilizing quantum-mechanical sum rules and spectral moments, while encouraging methods that incorporate these mechanisms through algebraic relations instead of complex wave equation solutions.

title: Grains and grain boundaries in single-layer graphene atomic patchwork quilts
abstract: The properties of polycrystalline materials are often dominated by the size of their grains and by the atomic structure of their grain boundaries. These effects should be especially pronounced in two-dimensional materials, where even a line defect can divide and disrupt a crystal. These issues take on practical significance in graphene, which is a hexagonal, two-dimensional crystal of carbon atoms. Single-atom-thick graphene sheets can now be produced by chemical vapour deposition on scales of up to metres, making their polycrystallinity almost unavoidable. Theoretically, graphene grain boundaries are predicted to have distinct electronic, magnetic, chemical and mechanical properties that strongly depend on their atomic arrangement. Yet because of the five-order-of-magnitude size difference between grains and the atoms at grain boundaries, few experiments have fully explored the graphene grain structure. Here we use a combination of old and new transmission electron microscopy techniques to bridge these length scales. Using atomic-resolution imaging, we determine the location and identity of every atom at a grain boundary and find that different grains stitch together predominantly through pentagon–heptagon pairs. Rather than individually imaging the several billion atoms in each grain, we use diffraction-filtered imaging to rapidly map the location, orientation and shape of several hundred grains and boundaries, where only a handful have been previously reported. The resulting images reveal an unexpectedly small and intricate patchwork of grains connected by tilt boundaries. By correlating grain imaging with scanning probe and transport measurements, we show that these grain boundaries severely weaken the mechanical strength of graphene membranes but do not as drastically alter their electrical properties. These techniques open a new window for studies on the structure, properties and control of grains and grain boundaries in graphene and other two-dimensional materials.
summary:
**New Study Reveals Surprising Grain Patterns in Graphene**

A team of scientists from various institutions, led by Pinshane Y. Huang, have made a significant breakthrough in understanding the atomic-level structure of grain boundaries in single-layer graphene. Their findings were published in *Nature*.

The study bridges a sizeable gap between atomic scale and macroscopic properties in two-dimensional materials like graphene, which is a one-atom-thick crystal of carbon. Previously, it was challenging to comprehensively explore grain structure due to the immense difference in size between grains and atoms at grain boundaries.

Using advanced electron microscope techniques, the researchers have managed to determine the exact location and identity of every atom at a graphene grain boundary. They discovered that these grains predominantly join through pentagon–heptagon pairs. The team was also able to quickly map and identify hundreds of grains and boundaries – a significant leap from the few previously reported ones.

The resulting images reveal an intricate patchwork of interconnected graphene grains, with tilt boundaries that could have major implications on the materials' mechanical and electrical properties. Although grain boundaries were found to weaken the mechanical strength of graphene membranes significantly, they did not cause as drastic changes in its electrical properties.

These findings open a new avenue for research on the structure, properties, and control of grains and grain boundaries in graphene and other two-dimensional materials.

title: Giant magnetoresistive in soft ferromagnetic multilayers
abstract: We show that the in-plane magnetoresistance of sandwiches of uncoupled ferromagnetic (${\mathrm{Ni}}_{81}$${\mathrm{Fe}}_{19}$,${\mathrm{Ni}}_{80}$${\mathrm{Co}}_{20}$,Ni) layers separated by ultrathin nonmagnetic metallic (Cu,Ag,Au) layers is strongly increased when the magnetizations of the two ferromagnetic layers are aligned antiparallel. The comparison between different ferromagnetic materials (alloys or pure elements) leads us to emphasize the role of bulk rather than interfacial spin-dependent scattering in these structures, in contrast to Fe/Cr multilayers.

title: Gapless spin-fluid ground state in a random quantum Heisenberg magnet
abstract:
We examine the spin-$S$ quantum Heisenberg magnet with Gaussian-random,
infinite-range exchange interactions. The quantum-disordered phase is accessed
by generalizing to $SU(M)$ symmetry and studying the large $M$ limit. For large
$S$ the ground state is a spin-glass, while quantum fluctuations produce a
spin-fluid state for small $S$. The spin-fluid phase is found to be generically
gapless - the average, zero temperature, local dynamic spin-susceptibility
obeys $\bar{\chi} (\omega ) \sim \log(1/|\omega|) + i (\pi/2) \mbox{sgn}
(\omega)$ at low frequencies. This form is identical to the phenomenological
`marginal' spectrum proposed by Varma {\em et. al.\/} for the doped cuprates.
summary:
"Physics Paper Discovers Gapless Spin-Fluid State in Quantum Heisenberg Magnet

A new study published in Physical Review Letters, authored by Subir Sachdev and Jinwu Ye, sheds light on a spin-fluid state within the quantum Heisenberg magnet. The researches examined a spin-$S$ model with Gaussian-random infinite-range exchange interactions, accessing a quantum-disordered phase through an $SU(M)$ symmetry analysis.

The ground state of this disordered phase was found to be a 'spin-glass' for large spins, but quantum fluctuations generate a 'spin-fluid' state in situations with small spin values. Strikingly, the spin-fluid phase exhibits a gapless property: the average local dynamic spin susceptibility follows a logarithmic form identical to the "marginal" spectrum first proposed for the doped cuprates by Varma and colleagues."

title: The world of the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation
abstract:
The cubic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation is one of the most-studied
nonlinear equations in the physics community.
 It describes a vast variety of phenomena from nonlinear waves to second-order
phase transitions, from superconductivity, superfluidity and Bose-Einstein
condensation to liquid crystals and strings in field theory. Our goal is to
give an overview of various phenomena described the complex Ginzburg-Landau
equation in one, two and three dimensions from the point of view of condensed
matter physicists. Our approach is to study the relevant solutions to get an
insight into nonequilibrium phenomena in spatially extended systems.
summary: In a new review published in Reviews of Modern Physics, authors Igor S. Aranson and Lorenz Kramer take a comprehensive look at the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation (CGL), a widely-studied nonlinear equation crucial to understanding various phenomena across physics, including superconductivity, superfluidity, Bose-Einstein condensation, and liquid crystals. The research aims to provide an overview of the diverse phenomena described by the CGL equation in one, two and three dimensions, focusing on insights gained from analyzing relevant solutions for a better understanding of nonequilibrium phenomena in extended systems.

title: Relaxation of Toroidal Plasma and Generation of Reverse Magnetic Fields
abstract: The spontaneous generation of reversed fields in toroidal plasmas is shown to be a consequence of relaxation under constraints. With perfect conductivity a topological constraint exists for each field line and the final state is not unique. With small departures from perfect conductivity, topological constraints are relaxed and the final state becomes unique. The onset of the reversed field and other features of this model agree well with observations on ZETA.
summary:
Paper Title: New Model Suggests Spontaneous Generation of Reverse Magnetic Fields in Toroidal Plasmas

Physicist J. B. Taylor's paper in Physical Review Letters reveals a groundbreaking theory about the spontaneous generation of reverse magnetic fields in toroidal plasmas. The study shows that this phenomenon occurs due to relaxation under constraints, which is crucial for understanding the behavior of these complex systems.

According to the paper, when perfect conductivity is assumed, each field line in a toroidal plasma is subject to a topological constraint, resulting in an ambiguous final state. However, when there are small departures from perfect conductivity, these constraints are relaxed, leading to a unique final state that aligns well with observations on ZETA, a significant experiment in magnetic fusion research. This work might provide valuable insights for designing more efficient and stable plasma confinement devices like magnetic fusion reactors.

title: Modeling molecular motors
abstract: The authors present general considerations and simple models for the operation of isothermal motors at small scales, in asymmetric environments. Their work is inspired by recent observations on the behavior of molecular motors in the biological realm, where chemical energy is converted into mechanical energy. A generic Onsager-like description of the linear (close to equilibrium) regime is presented, which exhibits structural differences from the usual Carnot engines. Turning to more explicit models for a single motor, the authors show the importance of the time scales involved and of the spatial dependence of the motor's chemical activity. Considering the situation in which a large collection of such motors operates together. The authors exhibit new features among which are dynamical phase transitions formally similar to paramagnetic-ferromagnetic and liquid-vapor transitions.
summary:
In the realm of physics, a groundbreaking study published in Reviews of Modern Physics offers new insights into molecular motors, the fascinating mechanisms that convert chemical energy into mechanical work within biological systems. The research by Frank Jülicher, Armand Ajdari, and Jacques Prost builds upon prior work examining these tiny engines, proposing simple models for their operation in asymmetric environments.

The paper presents a generic description based on Onsager-like theory, showing significant structural differences compared to traditional Carnot engines when operating in the linear regime. Furthermore, the study delves into explicit single motor models, emphasizing the significance of time scales and spatial chemical activity variations. Intriguingly, their findings suggest new, dynamic phase transitions resembling popular physical phenomena like paramagnetic-ferromagnetic or liquid-vapor transformations among large collections of these molecular motors.

title: Electron-hole excitations and optical spectra from first principles
abstract: We present a recently developed approach to calculate electron-hole excitations and the optical spectra of condensed matter from first principles. The key concept is to describe the excitations of the electronic system by the corresponding one- and two-particle Green's function. The method combines three computational techniques. First, the electronic ground state is treated within density-functional theory. Second, the single-particle spectrum of the electrons and holes is obtained within the $\mathrm{GW}$ approximation to the electron self-energy operator. Finally, the electron-hole interaction is calculated and a Bethe-Salpeter equation is solved, yielding the coupled electron-hole excitations. The resulting solutions allow the calculation of the entire optical spectrum. This holds both for bound excitonic states below the band gap, as well as for the resonant spectrum above the band gap. We discuss a number of technical developments needed for the application of the method to real systems. To illustrate the approach, we discuss the excitations and optical spectra of spatially isolated systems (atoms, molecules, and semiconductor clusters) and of extended, periodic crystals (semiconductors and insulators).
summary: In a breakthrough for condensed matter physics, a new method to calculate electron-hole excitations and optical spectra from first principles has been presented by Michael Rohlfing and Steven G. Louie in the Physical Review B journal. The approach utilizes Green's function to describe electronic system excitations, combining density-functional theory, the GW approximation for single-particle spectrum, and electron-hole interaction resolution to solve the Bethe-Salpeter equation. The method promises to calculate the entire optical spectrum, including both bound excitonic states in semiconductors and resonant spectrum above the band gap. The authors discuss technical advancements required for real-world applications and demonstrate the approach through spatially isolated systems and extended crystals, opening up avenues for a more comprehensive understanding of materials' optical properties.

title: Ab initiocalculation of phonon dispersions in semiconductors
abstract: The density-functional linear-response approach to lattice-dynamical calculations in semiconductors is presented in full detail. As an application, we calculate complete phonon dispersions for the elemental semiconductors Si and Ge, and for the III-V semiconductor compounds GaAs, AlAs, GaSb, and AlSb. Our results are in excellent agreement with experiments where available, and provide predictions where they are not. As a byproduct, we obtain real-space interatomic force constants for these materials, which are useful both for interpolating the dynamical matrices through the Brillouin zone, and as ingredients of approximate calculations for mixed systems such as alloys and microstructures. The possibility of studying these systems using the force constants of the pure materials relies on the so-called mass approximation, B i.e., on neglecting the dependence of the force constants upon composition. The accuracy of such an approximation is tested and found to be very good for cationic intermixing in binary semiconductors, while it is less so for anionic substitutions. The situation is intermediate in the case of elemental semiconductors.
summary:
New Calculation Method Accurately Predicts Phonon Dispersion in Semiconductors

Researchers at the Physical Review journal have presented a new method for calculating phonon dispersions in semiconductors, a significant advancement in materials science. The study, led by Paolo Giannozzi and his team, applies a density-functional linear-response approach to lattice-dynamical calculations for elemental semiconductors such as Si and Ge, as well as III-V semiconductor compounds like GaAs and AlSb.

The new method shows excellent agreement with experimental data where available and provides predictions where none exist. The research also produces real-space interatomic force constants that can be used for studying mixed systems like alloys and microstructures. The researchers test the accuracy of their method, finding it reliable for cationic intermixing in binary semiconductors but less so for anionic substitutions. This work enhances our understanding and potential for the development of new semiconductor materials.

title: A Collective Description of Electron Interactions: III. Coulomb Interactions in a Degenerate Electron Gas
abstract: The behavior of the electrons in a dense electron gas is analyzed quantum-mechanically by a series of canonical transformations. The usual Hamiltonian corresponding to a system of individual electrons with Coulomb interactions is first re-expressed in such a way that the long-range part of the Coulomb interactions between the electrons is described in terms of collective fields, representing organized "plasma" oscillation of the system as a whole. The Hamiltonian then describes these collective fields plus a set of individual electrons which interact with the collective fields and with one another via short-range screened Coulomb interactions. There is, in addition, a set of subsidiary conditions on the system wave function which relate the field and particle variables. The field-particle interaction is eliminated to a high degree of approximation by a further canonical transformation to a new representation in which the Hamiltonian describes independent collective fields, with ${n}^{\ensuremath{'}}$ degrees of freedom, plus the system of electrons interacting via screened Coulomb forces with a range of the order of the inter electronic distance. The new subsidiary conditions act only on the electronic wave functions; they strongly inhibit long wavelength electronic density fluctuations and act to reduce the number of individual electronic degrees of freedom by ${n}^{\ensuremath{'}}$. The general properties of this system are discussed, and the methods and results obtained are related to the classical density fluctuation approach and Tomonaga's one-dimensional treatment of the degenerate Fermi gas.
summary:
**Physicists Propose Novel Quantum Description of Electron Interactions**

In a new paper published in Physical Review, David Böhm and David Pines present a groundbreaking quantum mechanical analysis of electron interactions within a dense electron gas.

The scientists apply a series of canonical transformations to the standard Hamiltonian that describes individual electrons and their Coulomb interactions. Their aim was to rephrase Coulomb interactions in terms of collective fields, representing organized plasma oscillations within the system.

The resultant Hamiltonian now describes the collective plasma oscillations along with individual electrons interacting via short-range screened Coulomb interactions and interfacing with the collective fields. Subsidiary conditions on the wave function link the field and particle variables. The field-particle interaction is significantly reduced through an additional canonical transformation, leading to a Hamiltonian that represents independent collective fields with reduced individual electronic degrees of freedom by ${n}^{\prime}$.

The findings from this study not only offer new insights into the behavior of electrons in dense gas systems but also have potential connections to classical density fluctuation approaches and Tomonaga's one-dimensional treatments of degenerate Fermi gases.

title: Berry’s phase for energy bands in solids
abstract: Berry's phase is defined for the dynamics of electrons in periodic solids and an explicit formula is derived for it. Because of the special torus topology of the Brillouin zone a nonzero Berry phase is shown to exist in a one-dimensional parameter space. Symmetry of the Bloch functions in the Brillouin zone leads to the quantization of Berry's phase. A connection is established between the latter and the Wyckoff positions in the crystal in the framework of band representations of space groups. Berry's phase can therefore be used for labeling energy bands in solids.
summary:
Title: New Method for Labeling Energy Bands in Solids Unveiled

A groundbreaking study published in Physical Review Letters by researcher J. Žák reveals a new method to categorize and understand the behavior of electrons in solids using what's known as Berry's phase. This concept, initially applied to electron dynamics in periodic systems, has been adapted to provide an explicit formula for analyzing energy bands within the complex geometries of various solid state materials.

In this research, Berry's phase is particularly significant because it demonstrates quantization in a one-dimensional parameter space, a unique property due to the Brillouin zone's torus structure. The study also shows that the symmetry of Bloch functions within the Brillouin zone leads to quantized Berry phases and connections with Wyckoff positions in crystals, making it possible to use this phase for labeling energy bands in solids. This could potentially pave the way for better comprehension of solid state physics and advancements in materials science.

title: Recent Progress in Multiferroic Magnetoelectric Composites: from Bulk to Thin Films
abstract: Abstract Multiferroic magnetoelectric composite systems such as ferromagnetic‐ferroelectric heterostructures have recently attracted an ever‐increasing interest and provoked a great number of research activities, driven by profound physics from coupling between ferroelectric and magnetic orders, as well as potential applications in novel multifunctional devices, such as sensors, transducers, memories, and spintronics. In this Review, we try to summarize what remarkable progress in multiferroic magnetoelectric composite systems has been achieved in most recent few years, with emphasis on thin films; and to describe unsolved issues and new device applications which can be controlled both electrically and magnetically.

title: Experimental realization of the topological Haldane model with ultracold fermions
abstract: The Haldane model on a honeycomb lattice is a paradigmatic example of a Hamiltonian featuring topologically distinct phases of matter. It describes a mechanism through which a quantum Hall effect can appear as an intrinsic property of a band structure, rather than being caused by an external magnetic field. Although physical implementation has been considered unlikely, the Haldane model has provided the conceptual basis for theoretical and experimental research exploring topological insulators and superconductors. Here we report the experimental realization of the Haldane model and the characterization of its topological band structure, using ultracold fermionic atoms in a periodically modulated optical honeycomb lattice. The Haldane model is based on breaking both time-reversal symmetry and inversion symmetry. To break time-reversal symmetry, we introduce complex next-nearest-neighbour tunnelling terms, which we induce through circular modulation of the lattice position. To break inversion symmetry, we create an energy offset between neighbouring sites. Breaking either of these symmetries opens a gap in the band structure, which we probe using momentum-resolved interband transitions. We explore the resulting Berry curvatures, which characterize the topology of the lowest band, by applying a constant force to the atoms and find orthogonal drifts analogous to a Hall current. The competition between the two broken symmetries gives rise to a transition between topologically distinct regimes. By identifying the vanishing gap at a single Dirac point, we map out this transition line experimentally and quantitatively compare it to calculations using Floquet theory without free parameters. We verify that our approach, which allows us to tune the topological properties dynamically, is suitable even for interacting fermionic systems. Furthermore, we propose a direct extension to realize spin-dependent topological Hamiltonians.
summary:
**Ultracold Atom Physics Breakthrough: Scientists Realize Topological Haldane Model**

In a groundbreaking discovery published in Nature, a team of researchers led by Gregor Jotzu and Michael Messer have successfully realized the elusive Haldane model with ultracold fermionic atoms. This experimental achievement marks a significant step toward understanding topologically distinct phases of matter, which have been theoretically and experimentally explored for their potential in topological insulators and superconductors.

By breaking time-reversal symmetry and inversion symmetry using complex next-nearest-neighbor tunneling terms and energy offsets between neighboring sites respectively, the team opened a gap in the band structure, allowing them to probe its topology. The competition between the two broken symmetries led to a transition between topologically distinct regimes, which they mapped out experimentally and compared quantitatively to calculations using Floquet theory.

The researchers' approach, which allows for dynamic tuning of topological properties even in interacting fermionic systems, paves the way for future extensions to realize spin-dependent topological Hamiltonians. This work could potentially open new avenues for fundamental physics research and technological applications in quantum computing.

title: Electronic Structure of Pyrochlore Iridates: From Topological Dirac Metal to Mott Insulator
abstract: In 5d transition metal oxides such as the iridates, novel properties arise from the interplay of electron correlations and spin-orbit interactions. We investigate the electronic structure of the pyrochlore iridates, (such as Y$_{2}$Ir$_{2}$O$_{7}$) using density functional theory, LDA+U method, and effective low energy models. A remarkably rich phase diagram emerges on tuning the correlation strength U. The Ir magnetic moment are always found to be non-collinearly ordered. However, the ground state changes from a magnetic metal at weak U, to a Mott insulator at large U. Most interestingly, the intermediate U regime is found to be a Dirac semi-metal, with vanishing density of states at the Fermi energy. It also exhibits topological properties - manifested by special surface states in the form of Fermi arcs, that connect the bulk Dirac points. This Dirac phase, a three dimensional analog of graphene, is proposed as the ground state of Y$_{2}$Ir$_{2}$O$_{7}$ and related compounds. A narrow window of magnetic `axion' insulator, with axion parameter $θ=π$, may also be present at intermediate U. An applied magnetic field induces ferromagnetic order and a metallic ground state.
summary:
Headline:
New Study on Pyrochlore Iridates Highlights Transition from Topological Dirac Metal to Mott Insulator

Summary:
A new study published in arXiv by researchers Xiangang Wan, Ari M. Turner, Ashvin Vishwanath, and Sergey Y. Savrasov sheds light on the electronic structure of pyrochlore iridates, such as Y$_{2}$Ir$_{2}$O$_{7}$. The research utilizes density functional theory, LDA+U method, and effective low energy models to investigate these transition metal oxides known for their unique properties arising from the interplay of electron correlations and spin-orbit interactions. The study reveals a rich phase diagram as the correlation strength U is tuned, with findings including a non-collinearly ordered magnetic moment, a shift from a magnetic metal at weak U to a Mott insulator at large U, and an intriguing intermediate phase that transforms into a three-dimensional Dirac semi-metal with topological properties such as Fermi arcs connecting bulk Dirac points. This study proposes the Dirac phase as the ground state for Y$_{2}$Ir$_{2}$O$_{7}$ and similar compounds, and suggests a possible magnetic 'axion' insulator window at intermediate U strengths. An applied magnetic field leads to ferromagnetic order and a metallic ground state.

title: The Si-SiO<sub>2</sub>Interface - Electrical Properties as Determined by the Metal-Insulator-Silicon Conductance Technique
abstract: Measurements of the equivalent parallel conductance of metal-insulator-semiconductor (MIS) capacitors are shown to give more detailed and accurate information about interface states than capacitance measurements. Experimental techniques and methods of analysis are described. From the results of the conductance technique, a realistic characterization of the Si–SiO <inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> interface is developed. Salient features are: A continuum of states is found across the band gap of the silicon. Capture cross sections for holes and electrons are independent of energy over large portions of the band gap. The surface potential is subject to statistical fluctuations arising from various sources. The dominant contribution in the samples measured arises from a random distribution of surface charge. The fluctuating surface potential causes a dispersion of interface state time constants in the depletion region. In the weak inversion region the dispersion is eliminated by interaction between interface states and the minority carrier band. A single time constant results. From the experimentally established facts, equivalent circuits accurately describing the measurements are constructed.
summary:
Title: Revolutionary Study Reveals Deeper Insights into Si-SiO2 Interface Electrical Properties

The Bell System Technical Journal publishes a groundbreaking study by E. H. Nicollian and A. Goetzberger, exploring the electrical properties of the Si-SiO2 interface using the Metal-Insulator-Silicon (MIS) Conductance Technique. This approach, they find, provides more precise information about interface states compared to capacitance measurements, offering a clearer understanding of the Si-SiO2 interface.

The research reveals a continuous spectrum of states across the silicon band gap, with capture cross sections for holes and electrons showing independence from energy over substantial portions of the band gap. The study also highlights fluctuations in surface potential as the primary source of statistical variations at the interface, leading to a dispersion of interface state time constants in the depletion region.

This work paves the way for more accurate characterization of the Si-SiO2 interface and the construction of equivalent circuits that accurately describe these intricate electrical properties.

title: Quark gluon plasma and color glass condensate at RHIC? The Perspective from the BRAHMS experiment
abstract: We review the main results obtained by the BRAHMS collaboration on the properties of hot and dense hadronic and partonic matter produced in ultrarelativistic heavy ion collisions at RHIC. A particular focus of this paper is to discuss to what extent the results collected so far by BRAHMS, and by the other three experiments at RHIC, can be taken as evidence for the formation of a state of deconfined partonic matter, the so called quark-gluon-plasma (QGP). We also discuss evidence for a possible precursor state to the QGP, i.e. the proposed Color Glass Condensate.

title: The valley Hall effect in MoS <sub>2</sub> transistors
abstract: Using the valleys in monolayer MoS 2 The electronic structure of the two-dimensional material MoS 2 has two distinct “valleys” of energy that may help to carry information in future electronic devices. Mak et al. observed the so-called valley Hall effect in a monolayer of MoS 2 . The electrons from different valleys moved in opposite directions across the sample, with one valley being overrepresented with respect to the other. The scientists achieved this by shining circularly polarized light on the material, which created an imbalance in the population of the two valleys. The findings may enable practical applications in the newly formed field of valleytronics. Science , this issue p. 1489
summary:
**New Breakthrough in Valleytronics: Scientists Manipulate Electrons in Monolayer MoS2**

In a groundbreaking development for electronics, a team led by Kin Fai Mak and Kathryn L. McGill has successfully observed the "valley Hall effect" in a monolayer of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2). The scientists achieved this by shining circularly polarized light on the material, causing electrons from different energy valleys to move in opposite directions across the sample; one valley becoming overrepresented compared to the other.

The researchers believe that these findings could pave the way for practical applications in the emerging field of valleytronics, where manipulating and reading out information carried by distinct valleys in two-dimensional materials may be possible instead of using charge carriers as in traditional electronics. This progress marks a significant step forward in condensed matter physics research.

abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) Dirac point, where two Weyl points overlap in momentum space, is usually unstable and hard to realize. Here we show, based on the first-principles calculations and effective model analysis, that crystalline A(3)Bi (A = Na, K, Rb) are Dirac semimetals with bulk 3D Dirac points protected by crystal symmetry. They possess nontrivial Fermi arcs on the surfaces and can be driven into various topologically distinct phases by explicit breaking of symmetries. Giant diamagnetism, linear quantum magnetoresistance, and quantum spin Hall effect will be expected for such compounds.
summary:
Title: Scientists Discover New State of Matter in A(3)Bi Compounds

Summary:
A team of researchers from the Physical Review B have discovered a new state of matter known as Dirac semimetal in crystalline A(3)Bi, including A = Na, K, and Rb. The finding, based on first-principles calculations and effective model analysis, indicates these compounds host three-dimensional (3D) Dirac points protected by crystal symmetry. They also exhibit Fermi arcs on the surfaces, which can be manipulated into various topologically distinct phases by breaking symmetries. title: Inverse magnetocaloric effect in ferromagnetic Ni–Mn–Sn alloys
abstract: The magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in paramagnetic materials has been widely used for attaining very low temperatures by applying a magnetic field isothermally and removing it adiabatically. The effect can also be exploited for room-temperature refrigeration by using giant MCE materials1,2,3. Here we report on an inverse situation in Ni–Mn–Sn alloys, whereby applying a magnetic field adiabatically, rather than removing it, causes the sample to cool. This has been known to occur in some intermetallic compounds, for which a moderate entropy increase can be induced when a field is applied, thus giving rise to an inverse magnetocaloric effect4,5. However, the entropy change found for some ferromagnetic Ni–Mn–Sn alloys is just as large as that reported for giant MCE materials, but with opposite sign. The giant inverse MCE has its origin in a martensitic phase transformation that modifies the magnetic exchange interactions through the change in the lattice parameters.
summary:
New Study Discovers Inverse Magnetocaloric Effect in Ferromagnetic Ni–Mn–Sn Alloys

Researchers at the University of Barcelona and Max Planck Institute have found a new application for magnetic refrigeration in ferromagnetic materials. The team reports that applying a magnetic field adiabatically to Ni–Mn–Sn alloys causes the sample to cool, contrary to the usual method where cooling occurs when a magnetic field is removed. This 'inverse magnetocaloric effect' has been observed in some intermetallic compounds but is significant in these newly-identified alloys, with an entropy change as large as that reported for giant MCE materials but opposite in sign. The discovery could lead to the development of a new generation of room-temperature refrigeration systems based on this 'giant inverse magnetocaloric effect'. This breakthrough builds upon previous research into magnetic refrigeration and explores the potential for martensitic phase transformations to modify magnetic exchange interactions within materials, opening up new avenues in both condensed matter physics and materials science.

title: Antiferromagnetism. Theory of Superexchange Interaction
abstract: In this paper the general formalism of Kramers indicating the existence of superexchange interaction has been reduced, under simplifying assumptions, to the point where actual formulas for the interaction can be written down directly in terms of spin operators, with certain exchange and transition integrals as parameters. Two results of physical interest are the following: (a) superexchange must be expected to show the directional properties (as far as directional relations of interacting magnetic ions are concerned) of the orbitals in the outer shell of the non-magnetic connecting ions; and (b) the sign of the effective exchange integral depends upon the sign of the internal exchange coupling of an added electron on the magnetic ion.
summary:

The theory offers tangible formulas for this interaction, employing spin operators and specific exchange and transition integrals as parameters.

The study reveals two significant findings: firstly, the directional properties of interacting magnetic ions are influenced by the orbitals in the outer shell of non-magnetic connecting ions (a). Secondly, the sign of the effective exchange integral is determined by the internal exchange coupling of additional electrons on magnetic ions (b), a critical factor that opens possibilities for future research and applications in materials science.

title: High Efficiency Carrier Multiplication in PbSe Nanocrystals: Implications for Solar Energy Conversion
abstract: We demonstrate for the first time that impact ionization (II) (the inverse of Auger recombination) occurs with very high efficiency in semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs). Interband optical excitation of PbSe NCs at low pump intensities, for which less than one exciton is initially generated per NC on average, results in the formation of two or more excitons (carrier multiplication) when pump photon energies are more than 3 times the NC band gap energy. The generation of multiexcitons from a single photon absorption event is observed to take place on an ultrafast (picosecond) time scale and occurs with up to 100% efficiency depending upon the excess energy of the absorbed photon. Efficient II in NCs can be used to considerably increase the power conversion efficiency of NC-based solar cells.

This extraordinary carrier multiplication from a single photon event takes place in a mere picosecond and exhibits up to 100% efficiency with sufficient excess photon energy. The discovery of these efficient impact ionization processes in nanocrystals could potentially revolutionize the power conversion efficiency of solar cells based on such materials.

title: Origin of the Open Circuit Voltage of Plastic Solar Cells
abstract: A series of highly soluble fullerene derivatives with varying acceptor strengths (i.e., first reduction potentials) was synthesized and used as electron acceptors in plastic solar cells. These fullerene derivatives, methanofullerene [6,6]-phenyl C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM), a new azafulleroid, and a ketolactam quasifullerene, show a variation of almost 200 mV in their first reduction potential. The open circuit voltage of the corresponding devices was found to correlate directly with the acceptor strength of the fullerenes, whereas it was rather insensitive to variations of the work function of the negative electrode. These observations are discussed within the concept of Fermi level pinning between fullerenes and metals via surface charges.

title: Microwave oscillations of a nanomagnet driven by a spin-polarized current
abstract: The recent discovery that a spin-polarized electrical current can apply a large torque to a ferromagnet, through direct transfer of spin angular momentum, offers the possibility of manipulating magnetic-device elements without applying cumbersome magnetic fields. However, a central question remains unresolved: what type of magnetic motions can be generated by this torque? Theory predicts that spin transfer may be able to drive a nanomagnet into types of oscillatory magnetic modes not attainable with magnetic fields alone, but existing measurement techniques have provided only indirect evidence for dynamical states. The nature of the possible motions has not been determined. Here we demonstrate a technique that allows direct electrical measurements of microwave-frequency dynamics in individual nanomagnets, propelled by a d.c. spin-polarized current. We show that spin transfer can produce several different types of magnetic excitation. Although there is no mechanical motion, a simple magnetic-multilayer structure acts like a nanoscale motor; it converts energy from a d.c. electrical current into high-frequency magnetic rotations that might be applied in new devices including microwave sources and resonators.

title: Intrinsicn-type versusp-type doping asymmetry and the defect physics of ZnO
abstract: ZnO typifies a class of materials that can be doped via native defects in only one way: either n type or p type. We explain this asymmetry in ZnO via a study of its intrinsic defect physics, including ${\mathrm{Zn}}_{\mathrm{O}},$ ${\mathrm{Zn}}_{i},$ ${\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{O}},$ ${\mathrm{O}}_{i},$ and ${V}_{\mathrm{Zn}}$ and n-type impurity dopants, Al and F. We find that ZnO is n type at Zn-rich conditions. This is because (i) the Zn interstitial, ${\mathrm{Zn}}_{i},$ is a shallow donor, supplying electrons; (ii) its formation enthalpy is low for both Zn-rich and O-rich conditions, so this defect is abundant; and (iii) the native defects that could compensate the n-type doping effect of ${\mathrm{Zn}}_{i}$ (interstitial O, ${\mathrm{O}}_{i},$ and Zn vacancy, ${V}_{\mathrm{Zn}}),$ have high formation enthalpies for Zn-rich conditions, so these ``electron killers'' are not abundant. We find that ZnO cannot be doped p type via native defects $({\mathrm{O}}_{i},{V}_{\mathrm{Zn}})$ despite the fact that they are shallow (i.e., supplying holes at room temperature). This is because at both Zn-rich and O-rich conditions, the defects that could compensate p-type doping ${(V}_{\mathrm{O}}{,\mathrm{}\mathrm{Zn}}_{i},{\mathrm{Zn}}_{\mathrm{O}})$ have low formation enthalpies so these ``hole killers'' form readily. Furthermore, we identify electron-hole radiative recombination at the ${V}_{\mathrm{O}}$ center as the source of the green luminescence. In contrast, a large structural relaxation of the same center upon double hole capture leads to slow electron-hole recombination (either radiative or nonradiative) responsible for the slow decay of photoconductivity.
summary:
Article Headline:
"Unveiling the Asymmetry in ZnO Doping: Study Sheds Light on N-type Preference over P-type"

Newspaper Summary:
In a new study published by Physical Review. B, Condensed Matter, researchers led by Shengbai Zhang have shed light on the mysterious asymmetry of doping in ZnO, a common material used in electronics and optoelectronics. The research focuses on exploring the intrinsic defect physics of ZnO, including various native defects like ${\mathrm{Zn}}_{\mathrm{O}}$, ${\mathrm{Zn}}_{i}$, ${\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{O}}$, ${\mathrm{O}}_{i},$ and ${V}_{\mathrm{Zn}}$ as well as n-type impurities Al and F. The findings suggest that ZnO inherently favors n-type doping, a preference stemming from the abundance of low formation enthalpy shallow donor Zn interstitial, ${\mathrm{Zn}}_{i}$. This is further supported by the rarity of native defects that could potentially compensate this n-type effect under Zn-rich conditions, as they have high formation enthalpies and are thus not abundant. The study also reveals why ZnO cannot be doped p-type via native defects despite their shallow nature, suggesting that both Zn-rich and O-rich conditions result in the formation of defects that can compensate potential p-type doping, with low formation enthalpies leading to their abundance. Lastly, the study offers insights into the source of green luminescence in ZnO, identifying electron-hole recombination at the ${\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{O}}$ center as its origin, while also elucidating the slow decay of photoconductivity resulting from a large structural relaxation upon double hole capture at this same center.

title: The Chemical Structure of a Molecule Resolved by Atomic Force Microscopy
abstract: Atomic Imaging Within Adsorbed Molecules Scanning tunneling microscopy provides atomic resolution images of surfaces and adsorbed atoms, but imaging atoms within an organic molecule adsorbed on a surface is difficult because contrast is lacking in the states that determine the tunneling current. Atomic force microscopy should be able to resolve atoms through changes in short-range chemical forces, but resolution is lost if the scanning tip undergoes modifications or if it moves the molecule. Gross et al. (p. 1110 ) show that in situ functionalization of the tip—for example, with CO—can dramatically improve the resolution of images of pentacene molecules adsorbed on conducting surfaces, like copper, and nonconductors, like NaCl.

By in-situ functionalizing the tip of the AFM with CO, the researchers were able to significantly improve resolution on both conducting surfaces (like copper) and nonconductors (like NaCl), revolutionizing the field of atomic imaging within adsorbed molecules.

title: New perspectives for Rashba spin-orbit coupling.
abstract: In 1984, Bychkov and Rashba introduced a simple form of spin-orbit coupling to explain the peculiarities of electron spin resonance in two-dimensional semiconductors. Over the past 30 years, Rashba spin-orbit coupling has inspired a vast number of predictions, discoveries and innovative concepts far beyond semiconductors. The past decade has been particularly creative, with the realizations of manipulating spin orientation by moving electrons in space, controlling electron trajectories using spin as a steering wheel, and the discovery of new topological classes of materials. This progress has reinvigorated the interest of physicists and materials scientists in the development of inversion asymmetric structures, ranging from layered graphene-like materials to cold atoms. This Review discusses relevant recent and ongoing realizations of Rashba physics in condensed matter.

Duine delve into the latest advancements in the field of Rashba spin-orbit coupling. First introduced by Bychkov and Rashba in 1984 to explain electron spin resonance peculiarities in two-dimensional semiconductors, this concept has since sparked a wealth of research and innovation far beyond its initial scope.

The past decade has seen remarkable progress, with researchers successfully manipulating spin orientation while moving electrons, steering electron trajectories using spin as a wheel, and discovering new topological materials. The team's review highlights these advancements and discusses ongoing realizations of Rashba physics in condensed matter, rekindling interest among physicists and materials scientists in inversion asymmetric structures, ranging from graphene-like materials to cold atoms.

title: Characterization of Lorenz number with Seebeck coefficient measurement
abstract: In analyzing zT improvements due to lattice thermal conductivity (κL) reduction, electrical conductivity (σ) and total thermal conductivity (κTotal) are often used to estimate the electronic component of the thermal conductivity (κE) and in turn κL from κL = ∼ κTotal − LσT. The Wiedemann-Franz law, κE = LσT, where L is Lorenz number, is widely used to estimate κE from σ measurements. It is a common practice to treat L as a universal factor with 2.44 × 10−8 WΩK−2 (degenerate limit). However, significant deviations from the degenerate limit (approximately 40% or more for Kane bands) are known to occur for non-degenerate semiconductors where L converges to 1.5 × 10−8 WΩK−2 for acoustic phonon scattering. The decrease in L is correlated with an increase in thermopower (absolute value of Seebeck coefficient (S)). Thus, a first order correction to the degenerate limit of L can be based on the measured thermopower, |S|, independent of temperature or doping. We propose the equation: L=1.5+exp−|S|116 (where L is in 10−8 WΩK−2 and S in μV/K) as a satisfactory approximation for L. This equation is accurate within 5% for single parabolic band/acoustic phonon scattering assumption and within 20% for PbSe, PbS, PbTe, Si0.8Ge0.2 where more complexity is introduced, such as non-parabolic Kane bands, multiple bands, and/or alternate scattering mechanisms. The use of this equation for L rather than a constant value (when detailed band structure and scattering mechanism is not known) will significantly improve the estimation of lattice thermal conductivity.
summary:
New Study Finds Improved Way to Estimate Lattice Thermal Conductivity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

In a new study published in APL Materials, researchers from multiple institutions have proposed a revised method for estimating Lorenz number, a key factor in determining the electronic component of thermal conductivity. Previously, the widely used Wiedemann-Franz law established Lorenz number as a universal factor with a fixed value for degenerate semiconductors. However, researchers found significant deviations from this value, especially for non-degenerate semiconductors, which led to an equation that correlates Lorenz number with the thermopower (or absolute value of Seebeck coefficient). The new equation, L=1.5+exp−|S|116, provides a more accurate approximation for certain materials with different band structures and scattering mechanisms, which in turn should significantly improve the estimation of lattice thermal conductivity.

title: Upper Limit for the Critical Field in Hard Superconductors
abstract: An examination is presented of some recent reports dealing with the extremely high critical fields in certain hard superconductors. Observations of nuclear magnetic resonance in V/sub 3/Si and V/sub 3/Ga are shown to set a severe upper limit on the attainable critical field because of a reduction in the spin susceptibility of these materials in the superconducting state. Equations are derived for the maximum critical field using this limiting criterion. A table of maximum and estimated critical fields is presented for V/sub 2.95/ Ga, Nb/sub 3/ Sn, V/sub 3/Si, and V/sub 1.95/ Ga. It is concluded that the critical fields for these BETA -wolfran compounds are so high that they may be effectively limited at low temperatures by the normal-state paramagnetism. If this is the case, critical fields higher than about 300 kilogauss will not be realized unless materials can be discovered with high transition temperatures. (H.D.R.)
summary:
In a breakthrough study published in Physical Review Letters, physicist A.M. Clogston sets a new upper limit on the critical field in hard superconductors. The research explores the critical fields of V3Si and V3Ga, finding that nuclear magnetic resonance observations lead to a reduction in spin susceptibility in these materials upon transition into the superconducting state.

Based on these findings, Clogston derives equations for the maximum critical field, and presents a table comparing the estimated critical fields for several hard superconductors including V2.95Ga, Nb3Sn, V3Si, and V1.95Ga. The results suggest that the critical fields for BETA-wolfran compounds may be limited by normal-state paramagnetism at low temperatures, implying that significantly higher critical fields (above about 300 kilogauss) will not be achievable unless new superconducting materials with higher transition temperatures are discovered.

title: Thermal Conductance of an Individual Single-Wall Carbon Nanotube above Room Temperature
abstract:
The thermal properties of a suspended metallic single-wall carbon nanotube
(SWNT) are extracted from its high-bias (I-V) electrical characteristics over
the 300-800 K temperature range, achieved by Joule self-heating. The thermal
conductance is approximately 2.4 nW/K and the thermal conductivity is nearly
3500 W/m/K at room temperature for a SWNT of length 2.6 um and diameter 1.7 nm.
A subtle decrease in thermal conductivity steeper than 1/T is observed at the
upper end of the temperature range, which is attributed to second order
three-phonon scattering between two acoustic modes and one optical mode. We
discuss sources of uncertainty and propose a simple analytical model for the
SWNT thermal conductivity including length and temperature dependence.
summary:
Scientific Study Reveals High Thermal Conductivity in Single-Wall Carbon Nanotubes

A new study published in Nano Letters reports high thermal conductance in single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWNT), a discovery that could have significant implications for materials science. The research led by Eric Pop and colleagues measured the thermal properties of SWNT over the atmospheric temperature range, revealing an approximate thermal conductance of 2.4 nW/K and thermal conductivity of nearly 3500 W/m/K at room temperature.

The study sheds light on a subtle decrease in thermal conductivity observed in the upper end of the temperature range, attributed to second-order three-phonon scattering between acoustic and optical modes. The research proposes a simple analytical model for SWNT thermal conductivity including length and temperature dependence, potentially paving the way for novel applications in thermally conductive materials.
