The merged maps reveal an increase in eddy kinetic energy (EKE) levels by 30% compared to the T/P data alone. This detailed global mapping of ocean currents may help researchers better understand sources of oceanic EKE, particularly in the North Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

The research also indicates seasonal changes of eddy kinetic energy in several regions, including the northeastern Pacific, the northeastern and northwestern Atlantic, tropical oceans, and various bands in the Indian and western Pacific Oceans, and the northwestern Pacific. The detailed map offers a wealth of information on ocean circulation that could lead to improved climate models and predictions.

title: QuantumATK: an integrated platform of electronic and atomic-scale modelling tools
abstract: Abstract QuantumATK is an integrated set of atomic-scale modelling tools developed since 2003 by professional software engineers in collaboration with academic researchers. While different aspects and individual modules of the platform have been previously presented, the purpose of this paper is to give a general overview of the platform. The QuantumATK simulation engines enable electronic-structure calculations using density functional theory or tight-binding model Hamiltonians, and also offers bonded or reactive empirical force fields in many different parametrizations. Density functional theory is implemented using either a plane-wave basis or expansion of electronic states in a linear combination of atomic orbitals. The platform includes a long list of advanced modules, including Green’s-function methods for electron transport simulations and surface calculations, first-principles electron-phonon and electron-photon couplings, simulation of atomic-scale heat transport, ion dynamics, spintronics, optical properties of materials, static polarization, and more. Seamless integration of the different simulation engines into a common platform allows for easy combination of different simulation methods into complex workflows. Besides giving a general overview and presenting a number of implementation details not previously published, we also present four different application examples. These are calculations of the phonon-limited mobility of Cu, Ag and Au, electron transport in a gated 2D device, multi-model simulation of lithium ion drift through a battery cathode in an external electric field, and electronic-structure calculations of the composition-dependent band gap of SiGe alloys.

The authors provide a general overview of QuantumATK, highlighting its advanced modules that cover Green’s-function methods for electron transport simulations and surface calculations, first-principles electron-phonon and electron-photon couplings, simulation of atomic-scale heat transport, ion dynamics, spintronics, optical properties of materials, static polarization, and more. By integrating these different simulation engines into a single platform, the researchers aim to facilitate complex workflows by combining various simulation methods.

In addition to detailing the QuantumATK's features, the paper presents four application examples: calculations of the phonon-limited mobility of copper, silver, and gold; electron transport in a gated 2D device; lithium ion drift through a battery cathode under external electric field; and electronic structure calculations of composition-dependent band gaps in silicon–germanium (SiGe) alloys. These examples demonstrate the broad applicability and versatility of the QuantumATK platform within the realm of computational physics.

title: Calculation of critical layer thickness versus lattice mismatch for GexSi1−x/Si strained-layer heterostructures
abstract: A calculation of the critical layer thickness hc for growth of GexSi1−x strained layers on Si substrates is presented for 0≤x≤1.0. The present results are obtained assuming misfit dislocation generation is determined solely by energy balance. This approach differs therefore from previous theories (e.g., Matthews et al.), in which the absence of mechanical equilibrium for grown-in threading dislocations determines the onset of the generation of interfacial misfit dislocations. It is assumed that interfacial misfit dislocations will be generated when the areal strain energy density of the film exceeds the energy density associated with the formation of a screw dislocation at a distance from the free surface equal to the film thickness h. For films thicker than this critical value, screw (and edge) dislocations will be generated at the film/substrate interface. Values obtained for the critical thickness versus lattice mismatch are in excellent agreement with measurements of hc for GexSi1−x strained layers on Si substrates.

title: Thermal conductivity of individual silicon nanowires
abstract: The thermal conductivities of individual single crystalline intrinsic Si nanowires with diameters of 22, 37, 56, and 115 nm were measured using a microfabricated suspended device over a temperature range of 20–320 K. Although the nanowires had well-defined crystalline order, the thermal conductivity observed was more than two orders of magnitude lower than the bulk value. The strong diameter dependence of thermal conductivity in nanowires was ascribed to the increased phonon-boundary scattering and possible phonon spectrum modification.

The researchers attribute this anomaly to increased phonon-boundary scattering and potential phonon spectrum modifications in the nanowires. This study could open new avenues for understanding heat conduction at the nano-scale and pave the way for designing materials with tailored thermal properties.

title: Optical Response of High-Dielectric-Constant Perovskite-Related Oxide
abstract: Optical conductivity measurements on the perovskite-related oxide CaCu 3 Ti 4 O 12 provide a hint of the physics underlying the observed giant dielectric effect in this material. A low-frequency vibration displays anomalous behavior, implying that there is a redistribution of charge within the unit cell at low temperature. At infrared frequencies (terahertz), the value for the dielectric constant is ∼80 at room temperature, which is far smaller than the value of ∼10 5 obtained at lower radio frequencies (kilohertz). This discrepancy implies the presence of a strong absorption at very low frequencies due to dipole relaxation. At room temperature, the characteristic relaxation times are fast (≲500 nanoseconds) but increase dramatically at low temperature, suggesting that the large change in dielectric constant may be due to a relaxor-like dynamical slowing down of dipolar fluctuations in nanosize domains.

title: Space-Charge-Limited Currents in Solids
abstract: Currents, far in excess of ohmic currents, can be drawn through thin, relatively perfect insulating crystals. These currents are the direct analog of space-charge-limited currents in a vacuum diode. In actual crystals, the space-charge-limited currents are less than their theoretical value for an ideal crystal by the ratio of free to trapped carriers. Space-charge-limited currents become, therefore, a simple tool for measuring the imperfections in crystals even in the range of one part in ${10}^{15}$.The presence of traps not only reduces the magnitude of space-charge-limited currents, but also is likely to distort the shape of the current-voltage curve from an ideal square law to a much higher power dependence on voltage. The particular shape can be used to determine the energy distribution of traps.The presence of traps tends to uniformize the charge distribution between electrodes, to introduce a temperature dependence of the current, and to give rise to certain transient effects from which capture cross sections of traps may be computed.Space-charge-limited currents offer another mechanism for electrical breakdown in insulators.

title: Thermal Agitation of Electricity in Conductors
abstract: Statistical fluctuation of electric charge exists in all conductors, producing random variation of potential between the ends of the conductor. The effect of these fluctuations has been measured by a vacuum tube amplifier and thermocouple, and can be expressed by the formula ${\overline{I}}^{2}=(\frac{2kT}{\ensuremath{\pi}})\ensuremath{\int}{0}^{\ensuremath{\infty}}R(\ensuremath{\omega}){|Y(\ensuremath{\omega})|}^{2}d\ensuremath{\omega}$. $I$ is the observed current in the thermocouple, $k$ is Boltzmann's gas constant, $T$ is the absolute temperature of the conductor, $R(\ensuremath{\omega})$ is the real component of impedance of the conductor, $Y(\ensuremath{\omega})$ is the transfer impedance of the amplifier, and $\frac{\ensuremath{\omega}}{2\ensuremath{\pi}}=f$ represents frequency. The value of Boltzmann's constant obtained from the measurements lie near the accepted value of this constant. The technical aspects of the disturbance are discussed. In an amplifier having a range of 5000 cycles and the input resistance $R$ the power equivalent of the effect is $\frac{{\overline{V}}^{2}}{R}=0.8\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}{10}^{\ensuremath{-}16}$ watt, with corresponding power for other ranges of frequency. The least contribution of tube noise is equivalent to that of a resistance ${R}_{c}=1.5\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}\frac{{10}^{5}{i}_{p}}{\ensuremath{\mu}}$, where ${i}_{p}$ is the space current in milliamperes and $\ensuremath{\mu}$ is the effective amplification of the tube.

title: Chemical potential dependence of defect formation energies in GaAs: Application to Ga self-diffusion
abstract: We calculate absolute formation energies of native defects in GaAs. The formation energy and hence the equilibrium concentration of the defects depends strongly on the atomic chemical potentials of As and Ga as well as the electron chemical potential. For example, the Ga vacancy concentration changes by more than ten orders of magnitude as the chemical potentials of As and Ga vary over the thermodynamically allowed range. This result indicates that the rate of self-diffusion depends strongly on the surface-annealing conditions.

title: Effect of a nonzero temperature on quantum critical points in itinerant fermion systems
abstract: I reexamine the work of Hertz on quantum phase transitions in itinerant fermion systems. I determine when it is permissible to integrate out the fermions and analyze the critical phenomena via an effective bosonic theory in which only fluctuations of the ordering field are explicitly retained. By solving appropriate scaling equations I obtain the different regimes of behavior of the correlation length and free energy in the disordered phase of the effective bosonic theory. The results in many cases differ from those of Hertz, but make contact with more recent work on the dilute Bose gas. I briefly discuss the relevance of the results to heavy-fermion materials.

title: Theory of the half-filled Landau level
summary:
**Physics Study Sheds Light on Electron Behavior in Strong Magnetic Fields**

In a new paper published in Physical Review B, Condensed Matter, researchers led by B.I. Halperin, P.A. Lee, and N. Read propose an intriguing theory about two-dimensional electron systems under strong magnetic fields. The study examines the half-filled Landau level, which is equivalent to a system of fermions interacting with a Chern-Simons gauge field.

The research reveals that in the absence of impurity scattering, there should be a well-defined Fermi surface for these fermions. However, when considering gauge fluctuations, they found infrared divergent corrections to the quasiparticle propagator, leading to variations in the effective mass. The nature of the assumed electron-electron interaction impacts these corrections, with different types of interactions resulting in distinct outcomes, ranging from no infrared divergences for long-range interactions to power-law divergences for short-range repulsive interactions and logarithmic corrections for Coulomb interactions.

The team also discusses the implications of their findings for physical properties at the half-filled Landau level, including electronic specific heat and various other attributes. Furthermore, they propose a finite resistivity and make predictions for the energy gap in the fractional quantized Hall state at select filling fractions, as well as discussing the overall phase diagram that results from combining their theory with previous research focusing on impurity scattering regimes.

title: Ferreting out Tunneling: An Application to Indian Business Groups
abstract: Owners of business groups are often accused of expropriating minority shareholders by tunneling resources from firms where they have low cash flow rights to firms where they have high cash flow rights. In this paper we propose a general methodology to measure the extent of tunneling activities. The methodology rests on isolating and then testing the distinctive implications of the tunneling hypothesis for the propagation of earnings shocks across firms within a group. When we apply our methodology to data on Indian business groups, we find a significant amount of tunneling, much of it occurring via nonoperating components of profit.

title: Influence of quantum confinement on the electronic structure of the transition metal sulfide<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math>S<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow/><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>
abstract:
Bulk MoS2, a prototypical layered transition-metal dichalcogenide, is an
indirect band gap semiconductor. Reducing its size to a monolayer, MoS2
undergoes a transition to the direct band semiconductor. We support this
experimental observation by first principles calculations and show that quantum
confinement in layered d-electron dichalcogenides results in tuning the
electronic structure at the nanoscale. We further studied the properties of
related TmS2 nanolayers (Tm = W, Nb, Re) and show that the isotopological WS2
exhibits similar electronic properties, while NbS2 and ReS2 remain metallic
independent on size.
summary:
In a recent study published in Physical Review B, a team led by Agnieszka Kuc, Nourdine Zibouche, and Thomas Heine delve into the influence of quantum confinement on the electronic structure of transition metal sulfides (TMS). The research focuses on quantum dots, nanoscale semiconductors with properties different from their bulk counterparts.

The study investigates how reducing the size of a prototypical layered TMS, in this case MoS2, changes its electronic structure. It shows that shrinking MoS2 to a monolayer results in a direct band gap semiconductor, a shift from the indirect band gap observed in bulk MoS2.

The team's findings shed light on the quantum confinement effects in layered d-electron dichalcogenides and provide insights into the properties of related TM nanolayers (TM includes W, Nb, Re). Interestingly, while isotopological WS2 exhibits similar electronic properties, NbS2 and ReS2 remain metallic regardless of size. These results advance our understanding of quantum dots in materials science and may pave the way for future applications in nanoscience and nanotechnology.

title: Rock Magnetism
abstract: Rock Magnetism, first published in 1997, is a comprehensive treatment of fine particle magnetism and the magnetic properties of rocks. Starting from atomic magnetism and magnetostatic principles, the authors explain why domains and micromagnetic structures form in ferromagnetic crystals and how these lead to magnetic memory in the form of thermal, chemical and other remanent magnetizations. The phenomenal stability of these magnetizations, providing a record of plate tectonic motions over millions of years, is explained by thermal activation theory. One chapter is devoted to practical tests of domain state and paleomagnetic stability; another deals with pseudo-single-domain magnetism. The final four chapters place magnetism in the context of igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic, and extraterrestrial rocks. This book will be of great value to graduate students and researchers in geophysics and geology, particularly in paleomagnetism and rock magnetism, as well as physicists and electrical engineers interested in fine-particle magnetism and magnetic recording.
summary:
Title: Comprehensive Guide on Rock Magnetism Published in 1997

In a seminal work published by Cambridge University Press, geologists David J. Dunlop and Özden Özdemir delve into the intricacies of rock magnetism. The book elucidates fundamental principles of fine particle magnetism and magnetic properties found within rocks. From atomic magnetism to thermal activation theory, the authors explore the formation of domains and micromagnetic structures in ferromagnetic crystals, culminating in a robust record of plate tectonic movements over millions of years.

The book serves as an essential resource for graduate students and researchers in geophysics and geology, particularly those specializing in paleomagnetism and rock magnetism. It also offers insightful material for physicists and electrical engineers interested in fine-particle magnetism and magnetic recording. This wide-ranging guide offers valuable insights into the magnetism present in various rock types, from igneous to extraterrestrial.

title: Theory of graphitic boron nitride nanotubes
abstract: Based upon the similarities in properties between carbon- and BN-based (BN=boron nitride) materials, we propose that BN-based nanotubes can be stable and study their electronic structure. A simple Slater-Koster tight-binding scheme has been applied. All the BN nanotubes are found to be semiconducting materials. The band gaps are larger than 2 eV for most tubes. Depending on the helicity, the calculated band gap can be direct at \ensuremath{\Gamma} or indirect. In general, the larger the diameter of the nanotube the larger the band gap, with a saturation value corresponding to the calculated local-density-approximation band gap of hexagonal BN. The higher ionicity of BN is important in explaining the electronic differences between these tubes and similar carbon nanotubes.
summary:
In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review. B (Condensed Matter), renowned scientists Ángel Rubio, Jennifer L. Corkill, and Marvin L. Cohen propose that graphitic boron nitride nanotubes could be as stable as their carbon counterparts and exhibit intriguing electronic properties.

The researchers, building upon the shared characteristics between carbon and boron nitride materials, used a Slater-Koster tight-binding scheme to analyze the electronic structure of these potential nanotubes. Their findings suggest that all boron nitride nanotubes are semiconductors, most with band gaps exceeding 2 eV. The researchers also discovered that the band gap can be direct or indirect depending on the tubes' helicity. Furthermore, they found that larger diameter tubes tend to have larger band gaps, approaching the calculated local-density-approximation band gap of hexagonal boron nitride. Overall, the higher ionicity of BN is believed to play a crucial role in explaining the electronic differences between these tubes and carbon nanotubes, hinting at potential new applications for this promising material class.

title: Dirac Semimetal in Three Dimensions
abstract: We show that the pseudorelativistic physics of graphene near the Fermi level can be extended to three dimensional (3D) materials. Unlike in phase transitions from inversion symmetric topological to normal insulators, we show that particular space groups also allow 3D Dirac points as symmetry protected degeneracies. We provide criteria necessary to identify these groups and, as an example, present ab initio calculations of β-cristobalite BiO(2) which exhibits three Dirac points at the Fermi level. We find that β-cristobalite BiO(2) is metastable, so it can be physically realized as a 3D analog to graphene.
summary:
New Research Discovers Three-Dimensional "Dirac Material" Beyond Graphene

Physicists have found a new three-dimensional material that exhibits similar physics to graphene near the Fermi level, opening up possibilities for a new class of materials beyond two dimensions. The study on β-cristobalite BiO(2) reveals three "Dirac points" at the Fermi level, much like those found in graphene but in a three-dimensional structure. The findings could pave the way for a better understanding and potential applications of these pseudorelativistic materials, as the new 3D material, while metastable, is considered a promising 3D analog to graphene.

title: Polarization of Nuclei in Metals
abstract: A new method for polarizing nuclei, applicable only to metals, is proposed. It is shown that if the electron spin resonance of the conduction electrons is saturated, the nuclei will be polarized to the same degree they would be if their gyromagnetic ratio were that of the electron spin. This action results from the paramagnetic relaxation processes that occur by means of the hyperfine structure interaction between electron and nuclear spins. A shift of the electron spin resonance due to the same interaction will occur for large amounts of polarization and should provide a direct indication of the degree of polarization.
summary:
NewMetalNucleusPolarizationMethod Proposed

A groundbreaking method for polarizing nuclei, exclusively applicable to metals, has been proposed by physicist A. W. Overhauser in his paper "Polarization of Nuclei in Metals," published in Physical Review.

The research builds upon the Hyperfine structure concept as the underlying mechanism for inducing spin polarization within the metal's electrons. When the electron spin resonance of these conduction electrons is saturated, it causes nuclei to achieve a corresponding degree of polarization equivalent to if their own gyromagnetic ratio were that of an electron's.

This method relies on paramagnetic relaxation processes, triggered by the hyperfine structure interaction between electron and nuclear spins, which promises significant advances in the field of spin polarization for metallic materials. The research also proposes a shift of the electron spin resonance as a result of the same interaction, providing a potential direct measurement of the degree of polarization achieved.

title: Measurement of the Optical Conductivity of Graphene
abstract: Optical reflectivity and transmission measurements over photon energies between 0.2 and 1.2 eV were performed on single-crystal graphene samples on a SiO2 substrate. For photon energies above 0.5 eV, graphene yielded a spectrally flat optical absorbance of (2.3+/-0.2)%. This result is in agreement with a constant absorbance of pialpha, or a sheet conductivity of pie2/2h, predicted within a model of noninteracting massless Dirac fermions. This simple result breaks down at lower photon energies, where both spectral and sample-to-sample variations were observed. This "nonuniversal" behavior is explained by including the effects of doping and finite temperature, as well as contributions from intraband transitions.
summary:
Title: New Study Reveals Universal Optical Behavior in Single-Crystal Graphene

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kin Fai Mak have discovered a 'universal' optical behavior in single-crystal graphene. The team measured the optical conductivity of graphene samples, revealing a constant absorbance of 2.3% for photon energies above 0.5 eV - a value consistent with theoretical predictions based on massless Dirac fermions. This finding supports the notion that graphene's electronic properties can be well described by this simple model at high energies.

However, the team observed significant deviations from this universal behavior when examining lower photon energies. These inconsistencies were attributed to factors such as doping, temperature, and intraband transitions, signifying a more complex interplay of physical processes in graphene's optical properties at various energy levels.

This work further illuminates the intriguing electronic structure of graphene and its remarkable optical characterization as a material of great significance for both fundamental research and potential applications in optoelectronics.

title: Giant magnetoresistance in nonmultilayer magnetic systems
abstract: We have observed isotropic giant magnetoresistance (GMR) in nonmultilayer magnetic systems using granular magnetic solids. We show that GMR occurs in magnetically inhomogeneous media containing nonaligned ferromagnetic entities on a microscopic scale. The GMR is determined by the orientations of the magnetization axes, the density, and the size of the ferromagnetic entities.

title: Quantum‐mechanical condensed matter simulations with CRYSTAL
abstract: The latest release of the Crystal program for solid‐state quantum‐mechanical ab initio simulations is presented. The program adopts atom‐centered Gaussian‐type functions as a basis set, which makes it possible to perform all‐electron as well as pseudopotential calculations. Systems of any periodicity can be treated at the same level of accuracy (from 0D molecules, clusters and nanocrystals, to 1D polymers, helices, nanorods, and nanotubes, to 2D monolayers and slab models for surfaces, to actual 3D bulk crystals), without any artificial repetition along nonperiodic directions for 0–2D systems. Density functional theory calculations can be performed with a variety of functionals belonging to several classes: local‐density (LDA), generalized‐gradient (GGA), meta‐GGA, global hybrid, range‐separated hybrid, and self‐consistent system‐specific hybrid. In particular, hybrid functionals can be used at a modest computational cost, comparable to that of pure LDA and GGA formulations, because of the efficient implementation of exact nonlocal Fock exchange. Both translational and point‐symmetry features are fully exploited at all steps of the calculation, thus drastically reducing the corresponding computational cost. The various properties computed encompass electronic structure (including magnetic spin‐polarized open‐shell systems, electron density analysis), geometry (including full or constrained optimization, transition‐state search), vibrational properties (frequencies, infrared and Raman intensities, phonon density of states), thermal properties (quasi‐harmonic approximation), linear and nonlinear optical properties (static and dynamic [hyper]polarizabilities), strain properties (elasticity, piezoelectricity, photoelasticity), electron transport properties (Boltzmann, transport across nanojunctions), as well as X‐ray and inelastic neutron spectra. The program is distributed in serial, parallel, and massively parallel versions. In this paper, the original developments that have been devised and implemented in the last 4 years (since the distribution of the previous public version, Crystal14 , occurred in December 2013) are described. This article is categorized under: Software > Quantum Chemistry Structure and Mechanism > Computational Materials Science Electronic Structure Theory > Density Functional Theory

Headline:
New Quantum-Mechanical Simulation Program Offers Advancements in Condensed Matter Research

Summary:
A team of researchers, led by Roberto Dovesi, have introduced an updated version of the Crystal program for quantum-mechanical simulations in solid-state materials science. The software, which can handle systems ranging from molecules to 3D crystals, boasts improvements in computational efficiency and versatility. It allows for density functional theory calculations with various functional types—including local-density, generalized-gradient, hybrid, range-separated hybrid, and self-consistent system-specific hybrid – all achieved through efficient implementations of exact nonlocal Fock exchange and exploitation of translational and point symmetry features. The updated Crystal program is expected to aid in the computational analysis of electronic structure, geometry, vibrational properties, thermal and optical properties, strain properties, electron transport properties, and X-ray and neutron spectra, ultimately advancing research in computational materials science.

title: Observation of many-body localization of interacting fermions in a quasirandom optical lattice
abstract: Making interacting atoms localize Disorder can stop the transport of noninteracting particles in its tracks. This phenomenon, known as Anderson localization, occurs in disordered solids, as well as photonic and cold atom settings. Interactions tend to make localization less likely, but disorder, interactions, and localization may coexist in the so-called many-body localized state. Schreiber et al. detect many-body localization in a one-dimensional optical lattice initially filled with atoms occupying alternating sites. Externally induced disorder and interactions prevented the system from evolving quickly to a state with a single atom on each site. Science , this issue p. 842

Title: Scientists Observe Unique State of Matter in Quasirandom Optical Lattice

In a groundbreaking study published in Science, an international team led by Michael Schreiber has successfully observed many-body localization in a one-dimensional optical lattice filled with atoms. The researchers created this state by combining externally-induced disorder and interactions to prevent the system from evolving quickly towards a uniform distribution of atoms. This achievement marks significant progress in understanding condensed matter physics, building upon previous work that described Anderson localization in disordered solids and photonic and cold atom systems. The research could have far-reaching implications for exploring novel quantum many-body phenomena and technologies.

title: Non-equilibrium critical phenomena and phase transitions into absorbing states
abstract:
This review addresses recent developments in nonequilibrium statistical
physics. Focusing on phase transitions from fluctuating phases into absorbing
states, the universality class of directed percolation is investigated in
detail. The survey gives a general introduction to various lattice models of
directed percolation and studies their scaling properties, field-theoretic
aspects, numerical techniques, as well as possible experimental realizations.
In addition, several examples of absorbing-state transitions which do not
belong to the directed percolation universality class will be discussed. As a
closely related technique, we investigate the concept of damage spreading. It
is shown that this technique is ambiguous to some extent, making it impossible
to define chaotic and regular phases in stochastic nonequilibrium systems.
Finally, we discuss various classes of depinning transitions in models for
interface growth which are related to phase transitions into absorbing states.
summary:
Title: Advances in Non-Equilibrium Critical Phenomena Unveiled

In a new review published in Advances In Physics, physicist Haye Hinrichsen delves into the complex world of nonequilibrium statistical physics. The focus is on phase transitions from fluctuating phases into absorbing states, particularly within the universality class of Directed Percolation.

The paper provides a comprehensive exploration of various lattice models for Directed Percolation, examining their scaling properties, field-theoretic aspects, and numerical techniques. It also highlights potential experimental realizations and discusses absorbing-state transitions that do not align with the Directed Percolation universality class.

Furthermore, Hinrichsen investigates the concept of damage spreading but finds it to be ambiguous, presenting challenges in defining chaotic and regular phases in stochastic nonequilibrium systems. The review concludes by discussing various classes of depinning transitions in models for interface growth related to phase transitions into absorbing states.

title: Spin Ice State in Frustrated Magnetic Pyrochlore Materials
abstract: A frustrated system is one whose symmetry precludes the possibility that every pairwise interaction (“bond”) in the system can be satisfied at the same time. Such systems are common in all areas of physical and biological science. In the most extreme cases, they can have a disordered ground state with “macroscopic” degeneracy; that is, one that comprises a huge number of equivalent states of the same energy. Pauling's description of the low-temperature proton disorder in water ice was perhaps the first recognition of this phenomenon and remains the paradigm. In recent years, a new class of magnetic substance has been characterized, in which the disorder of the magnetic moments at low temperatures is precisely analogous to the proton disorder in water ice. These substances, known as spin ice materials, are perhaps the “cleanest” examples of such highly frustrated systems yet discovered. They offer an unparalleled opportunity for the study of frustration in magnetic systems at both an experimental and a theoretical level. This article describes the essential physics of spin ice, as it is currently understood, and identifies new avenues for future research on related materials and models.
summary: In the field of Physics and Condensed Matter Physics, a groundbreaking study published in Science reveals new insights into Spin Ice - a magnetic state found in Pyrochlore materials that closely resembles the disordered proton disorder in water ice. The work, lead by S.T. Bramwell and Michel J.P. Gingras, highlights the unique properties of these materials as "the cleanest" examples yet discovered of highly frustrated systems. The article provides a thorough analysis of Spin Ice, offering directions for future research in magnetic systems, aiming to uncover more about frustration - a concept common across multiple scientific disciplines.
allAuthors: S. T. Bramwell; Michel J. P. Gingras

title: Fowler-Nordheim Tunneling into Thermally Grown SiO2
abstract: Electronic conduction in thermally grown SiO2 has been shown to be limited by Fowler-Nordheim emission, i.e., tunneling of electrons from the vicinity of the electrode Fermi level through the forbidden energy gap into the conduction band of the oxide. Fowler-Nordheim characteristics have been observed over more than five decades of current for emission from Si, Al, and Mg. If previously measured values of the barrier heights are used, the slopes of the Fowler-Nordheim characteristics (log J/E2 vs 1/E) imply values of the relative effective mass in the forbidden band of about 0.4. These values take into account corrections for image-force barrier lowering and for temperature effects. The absolute values of the currents are lower by a factor of five to ten than the theoretically expected values, probably due to trapping effects. The temperature dependence of the current was found to follow the theoretical curve from 80°–420°K. However, an inconsistent relative effective mass of about 0.95 had to be assumed. These results are believed to provide the most complete examination of the Fowler-Nordheim-emission theory.
summary:
Headline: Breakthrough in Field Electron Emission Science: Study reveals new insights on Fowler-Nordheim Tunneling into Thermally Grown SiO2

Summary: A groundbreaking study led by researchers M. Lenzlinger and E. H. Snow, published in the Journal of Applied Physics, has provided an extensive examination of Fowler-Nordheim emission - a crucial concept in field electron emission science. The research reveals that electronic conduction in thermally grown SiO2 is limited by this emission mechanism, where electrons tunnel from the electrode's Fermi level through the forbidden energy gap into the oxide's conduction band. The findings suggest a relative effective mass of about 0.4 in the forbidden band, taking into account corrections for image-force barrier lowering and temperature effects. However, the absolute values of current are found to be significantly lower than theoretically expected, possibly due to trapping effects. The study's temperature dependence of the current follows theoretical curves from 80°–420°K, although an inconsistent relative effective mass of about 0.95 had to be assumed. This research is believed to provide the most complete examination of Fowler-Nordheim emission theory to date, with potential implications for condensed matter physics and electron studies.

title: Contrasting Eastern-Pacific and Central-Pacific Types of ENSO
abstract: Abstract Surface observations and subsurface ocean assimilation datasets are examined to contrast two distinct types of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) in the tropical Pacific: an eastern-Pacific (EP) type and a central-Pacific (CP) type. An analysis method combining empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis and linear regression is used to separate these two types. Correlation and composite analyses based on the principal components of the EOF were performed to examine the structure, evolution, and teleconnection of these two ENSO types. The EP type of ENSO is found to have its SST anomaly center located in the eastern equatorial Pacific attached to the coast of South America. This type of ENSO is associated with basinwide thermocline and surface wind variations and shows a strong teleconnection with the tropical Indian Ocean. In contrast, the CP type of ENSO has most of its surface wind, SST, and subsurface anomalies confined in the central Pacific and tends to onset, develop, and decay in situ. This type of ENSO appears less related to the thermocline variations and may be influenced more by atmospheric forcing. It has a stronger teleconnection with the southern Indian Ocean. Phase-reversal signatures can be identified in the anomaly evolutions of the EP-ENSO but not for the CP-ENSO. This implies that the CP-ENSO may occur more as events or epochs than as a cycle. The EP-ENSO has experienced a stronger interdecadal change with the dominant period of its SST anomalies shifted from 2 to 4 yr near 1976/77, while the dominant period for the CP-ENSO stayed near the 2-yr band. The different onset times of these two types of ENSO imply that the difference between the EP and CP types of ENSO could be caused by the timing of the mechanisms that trigger the ENSO events.
summary:
Headline: New Study Reveals Distinct Types of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) in Tropical Pacific

Summary: In a recent study published in Journal of Climate, researchers Hsun‐Ying Kao and Jin‐Yi Yu have identified two distinct types of ENSO - eastern-Pacific (EP) and central-Pacific (CP) - based on surface observations and subsurface ocean assimilation data. The EP type is characterized by its SST anomaly center located in the east equatorial Pacific, associated with basinwide thermocline and surface wind variations, and showing a strong teleconnection with the tropical Indian Ocean. In contrast, the CP type has most of its anomalies confined in the central Pacific, tends to onset, develop, and decay locally, is less related to thermocline variations, and exhibits a stronger connection with the southern Indian Ocean. The study suggests that the differences between these two types could be caused by the timing of mechanisms triggering ENSO events, bringing new insights into this crucial climatological phenomenon.
allAuthors: Hsun‐Ying Kao; Jin‐Yi Yu

title: A Tunable Kondo Effect in Quantum Dots
abstract: A tunable Kondo effect has been realized in small quantum dots. A dot can be switched from a Kondo system to a non-Kondo system as the number of electrons on the dot is changed from odd to even. The Kondo temperature can be tuned by means of a gate voltage as a single-particle energy state nears the Fermi energy. Measurements of the temperature and magnetic field dependence of a Coulomb-blockaded dot show good agreement with predictions of both equilibrium and nonequilibrium Kondo effects.
summary:
Headline: Quantum Dot Revolutionizes Control of 'Kondo Effect' in Condensed Matter Physics

Summary:
A groundbreaking study published in Science by researchers S.M. Cronenwett, Tjerk H. Oosterkamp, and Leo P. Kouwenhoven has brought about a remarkable advancement in condensed matter physics. The team successfully realized a tunable 'Kondo effect' in small quantum dots, offering unprecedented control over this notable phenomenon. By altering the number of electrons on the dot from odd to even, they managed to switch a dot between a Kondo system and a non-Kondo system. Furthermore, the researchers demonstrated an ability to tune the 'Kondo temperature' via a gate voltage as a single-particle energy state neared the Fermi energy. The findings provide significant validation of both equilibrium and nonequilibrium Kondo effect theories, potentially opening new avenues for further exploration in this exciting field.

title: Electronic Structure and Stability of Semiconducting Graphene Nanoribbons
abstract: We present a systematic density functional theory study of the electronic properties, optical spectra, and relative thermodynamic stability of semiconducting graphene nanoribbons. We consider ribbons with different edge nature including bare and hydrogen-terminated ribbons, several crystallographic orientations, and widths up to 3 nm. Our results can be extrapolated to wider ribbons providing a qualitative way of determining the electronic properties of ribbons with widths of practical significance. We predict that in order to produce materials with band gaps similar to Ge or InN, the width of the ribbons must be between 2 and 3 nm. If larger bang gap ribbons are needed (like Si, InP, or GaAs), their width must be reduced to 1-2 nm. According to the extrapolated inverse power law obtained in this work, armchair carbon nanoribbons of widths larger than 8 nm will present a maximum band gap of 0.3 eV, while for ribbons with a width of 80 nm the maximum possible band gap is 0.05 eV. For chiral nanoribbons the band gap oscillations rapidly vanish as a function of the chiral angle indicating that a careful design of their crystallographic nature is an essential ingredient for controlling their electronic properties. Optical excitations show important differences between ribbons with and without hydrogen termination and are found to be sensitive to the carbon nanoribbon width. This should provide a practical way of revealing information on their size and the nature of their edges.
summary:
Headline:
"New Study Predicts Optimal Widths for Semiconducting Graphene Nanoribbons to Achieve Specific Band Gaps"

Scuseria explore the electronic properties, optical spectra, and thermodynamic stability of graphene nanoribbons. title: Interfaces in crystalline materials
abstract: A brief review of the theoretical state of the art in the field of semiconductor interfaces is presented. It is shown that the important factor controlling the different semiconductor barrier heights is the density of states associated with the semiconductor dangling-bonds. passivated semiconductor surfaces present saturated dangling-bonds and have modified barrier heights. Results for hydrogen-passivated GaAs (110)-surfaces are presented; it is shown that the Schottky-barrier height formed by the deposition of a K-layer is sustantially changed by the hydrogen-passivation.
summary:
Title: Breakthrough in Semiconductor Research: Passivating Dangling Bonds Affects Barrier Heights

In the world of materials science, a groundbreaking study reveals the significance of dangling bonds in controlling barrier heights across various semiconductor interfaces. The research, published in SPIE's Proceedings, shows that the density of states associated with these bonds plays a crucial role. The authors, F. Flóres, R. Saiz-Pardo, and Raúl Rincón, have further demonstrated how passivating semiconductor surfaces can modify barrier heights through the saturation of dangling bonds. Results from hydrogen-passivated GaAs (110)-surfaces are presented, indicating that the Schottky-barrier height formed by deposition of a K-layer is significantly altered due to hydrogen passivation. This research could lead to improved understanding and manipulation of semiconductor interfaces for various applications in electronics and optoelectronics.

title: Confinement of Electrons to Quantum Corrals on a Metal Surface
abstract: A method for confining electrons to artificial structures at the nanometer lengthscale is presented. Surface state electrons on a copper(111) surface were confined to closed structures (corrals) defined by barriers built from iron adatoms. The barriers were assembled by individually positioning iron adatoms with the tip of a 4-kelvin scanning tunneling microscope (STM). A circular corral of radius 71.3 Å was constructed in this way out of 48 iron adatoms. Tunneling spectroscopy performed inside of the corral revealed a series of discrete resonances, providing evidence for size quantization. STM images show that the corral's interior local density of states is dominated by the eigenstate density expected for an electron trapped in a round two-dimensional box.
summary:
New Method Confines Electrons to Nanoscale Quantum Corrals on a Metal Surface

The scientists Michael F. Crommie, Christopher P. Lutz, and D. M. Eigler, as reported in Science journal, have developed a groundbreaking method to confine electrons within artificial structures at the nanometer scale. By using a 4-kelvin scanning tunneling microscope (STM), they constructed a circular corral of 48 iron adatoms on copper(111) surface.

The corral, with a radius of 71.3 Å, hosts unique electrons known as surface state electrons. Tunneling spectroscopy evidence shows that these electrons exhibit size quantization within the confined structure, which is essential for quantum computing and nanotechnology research. STM images reveal a local density of states in the corral's interior similar to an electron trapped in a two-dimensional square box, marking a significant step towards manipulating electrons at the quantum level.

title: First-principles study of native point defects in ZnO
abstract: The characterization of native point defects in ZnO is still a question of debate. For example, experimental evidence for ZnO with an excess of Zn is inconclusive as to whether the dominant defects are metal interstitials or oxygen vacancies. This information is essential to understand the behavior of the material and to tailor its numerous technological applications. We use the first-principles pseudopotential method to determine the electronic structure, atomic geometry, and formation energy of native point defects in ZnO. Interstitials, vacancies, and antisites in their relevant charge states are considered and the effects of dopants are also discussed. The results show that both the Zn and O vacancies are the relevant defects in ZnO. We also propose a possible transition mechanism and defect center responsible for the experimentally observed green luminescence.
summary:
**Breakthrough Study Uncovers Native Defects in Widespread Material ZnO**

A groundbreaking study by Kohan et al., published in Physical Review B, sheds light on the elusive nature of native point defects in the popular semiconductor Zinc Oxide (ZnO). The research uses a first-principles pseudopotential method to explore different defects and their implications for the material's behavior and technological applications.

Previous experiments have been inconclusive on whether ZnO predominantly hosts metal interstitials or oxygen vacancies, but this new work demonstrates that both types of native point defects are relevant in ZnO. The findings also propose a potential transition mechanism and defect center linked to the green luminescence commonly observed in ZnO-based materials. This study could pave the way for optimizing ZnO's numerous technological applications, including electronics, optoelectronics, and photocatalysis.

title: Ground-State Energy of a Many-Fermion System. II
abstract: The perturbation series for the ground-state energy of a many-fermion system is investigated to arbitrary order for the "isotropic" case. This is the case of over-all spherical symmetry, both in the interaction and in the unperturbed single particle energies. It is shown that for spin one-half fermions the Brueckner-Goldstone perturbation series is valid to all orders in the perturbation. For spins greater than one-half it is in general incorrect even in the isotropic case, unless the interactions are spin independent.The discussion to arbitrary order in the interaction is carried out by means of a Feynman-like propagator formalism, which is developed in detail.
summary:
Title: Physicists Challenge Fermion Energy Model with New Insights

A new study published in Physical Review by J. M. Luttinger and John Ward challenges conventional views on the energy of many-fermion systems. The research focuses on "isotropic" cases, where particles and interactions exhibit overall spherical symmetry.

The paper investigates the perturbation series for ground-state energy in this context and finds that the Brueckner-Goldstone perturbation series remains valid for spin-half fermions, but not necessarily for spins greater than half. Intriguingly, they also discovered that for cases with interactions dependent on spins other than independent ones, their model tends to be incorrect even in isotropic scenarios.

Luttinger and Ward's study is a significant contribution to the field of quantum physics, as it further explores the complexities of many-fermion systems through an innovative Feynman-like propagator formalism, shedding light on the subtleties that emerge when considering interactions dependent on spins.

title: Atomic View of Surface Self-Diffusion: Tungsten on Tungsten
abstract: Surface diffusion of tungsten adatoms on several smooth, low-index planes of the tungsten lattice has for the first time been followed by direct observation of individual atoms in the field-ion microscope. Contrary to expectation, the mobility at room temperature is found to increase in the order (211) &gt; (321) ∼ (110) &gt; (310) ∼ (111). Migrating atoms are reflected at the boundaries of the (110), (211), and (321) planes; on the latter two, motion along atomic rows is favored over diffusion across lattice steps. From quantitative determinations of the rate of change of the mean-square displacement, diffusion coefficients are obtained as follows: (110), D=3×10−2exp(−22 000/RT)cm2/sec; (321), 1×10−3exp(−20 000/RT); (211), 2×10−7exp(−13 000/RT). Differences in diffusion on the (211) and (321), planes of very similar structure, suggest a weakening of interatomic forces at lattice edges.
summary:
New Research Reveals Tungsten's Atomic Mobility on Specific Surfaces

In a groundbreaking study published in The Journal of Chemical Physics called "Atomic View of Surface Self-Diffusion: Tungsten on Tungsten," researchers Gert Ehrlich and F. G. Hudda have, for the first time, directly observed the movement of individual tungsten atoms using a field ion microscope. The results challenge previous expectations as the mobility of tungsten adatoms at room temperature increases in the order (211) > (321) ≈ (110) > (310) ≈ (111).

The research provides insights into the migration of atoms and their behavior on different planes of the tungsten lattice, with a significant finding being that migrating atoms are reflected at boundaries of the (110), (211), and (321) planes, suggesting a preference for motion along atomic rows over diffusion across steps. Through quantitative analysis of displacement rates, the scientists determine distinct lattice diffusion coefficients for these surfaces.

Interestingly, differences in diffusion on similarly-structured (211) and (321) planes suggest a weakening of interatomic forces at lattice edges, offering valuable insights into the behavior of this important metal. The study adds to our understanding of surface self-diffusion and its significance in various scientific disciplines.

title: CaCu 3 Ti 4 O 12 : One-step internal barrier layer capacitor
abstract: There has been much recent interest in a so-called “giant-dielectric phenomenon” displayed by an unusual cubic perovskite-type material, CaCu3Ti4O12; however, the origin of the high permittivity has been unclear [M. A. Subramanian, L. Dong, N. Duan, B. A. Reisner, and A. W. Sleight, J. Solid State Chem. 151, 323 (2000); C. C. Homes, T. Vogt, S. M. Shapiro, S. Wakimoto, and A. P. Ramirez, Science 293, 673 (2001); A. P. Ramirez, M. A. Subramanian, M. Gardel, G. Blumberg, D. Li, T. Vogt, and S. M. Shapiro, Solid State Commun. 115, 217 (2000)]. Impedance spectroscopy on CaCu3Ti4O12 ceramics demonstrates that they are electrically heterogeneous and consist of semiconducting grains with insulating grain boundaries. The giant-dielectric phenomenon is therefore attributed to a grain boundary (internal) barrier layer capacitance (IBLC) instead of an intrinsic property associated with the crystal structure. This barrier layer electrical microstructure with effective permittivity values in excess of 10 000 can be fabricated by single-step processing in air at ∼1100 °C. CaCu3Ti4O12 is an attractive option to the currently used BaTiO3-based materials which require complex, multistage processing routes to produce IBLCs of similar capacity.
summary:
"New Breakthrough in Material Science: Study Confirms High Permittivity of Rare Cubic Perovskite Is Due to Grain Boundary Capacitance"

In a groundbreaking study published in Applied Physics Letters, researchers have discovered that high permittivity levels observed in CaCu3Ti4O12, a unique cubic perovskite-type material, are not intrinsic to the crystal structure as previously believed. Instead, they have determined that this so-called "giant-dielectric phenomenon" is due to a grain boundary barrier layer capacitance (IBLC). The study by Derek C. Sinclair and colleagues demonstrates that these materials consist of semiconducting grains with insulating grain boundaries, shedding light on the mysterious high permittivity in CaCu3Ti4O12. This single-step barrier layer electrical microstructure offers an appealing alternative to currently used BaTiO3-based materials requiring intricate, multistage processing, potentially revolutionizing the field of capacitor technology.

abstract: Self-excited transverse electromagnetic waves which involve only the electrons were found to exist in plasmas provided the velocity distribution is sufficiently anisotropic. title: Hall Effect in Ferromagnetics
abstract: Both the unusually large magnitude and strong temperature dependence of the extraordinary Hall effect in ferromagnetic materials can be understood as effects of the spin-orbit interaction of polarized conduction electrons. It is shown that the interband matrix elements of the applied electric potential energy combine with the spin-orbit perturbation to give a current perpendicular to both the field and the magnetization. Since the net effect of the spin-orbit interaction is proportional to the extent to which the electron spins are aligned, this current is proportional to the magnetization. The magnitude of the Hall constant is equal to the square of the ordinary resistivity multiplied by functions that are not very sensitive to temperature and impurity content. The experimental results behave in such a way also.
summary:
Paper title: "Understanding the Extraordinary Hall Effect in Ferromagnetics"

In a new study published in Physical Review, Robert Karplus and J. M. Luttinger propose an explanation for the unusual behavior of the Hall effect in ferromagnetic materials. The researchers suggest that this phenomenon can be attributed to the spin-orbit interaction of polarized conduction electrons. By considering the combination of interband matrix elements of electric potential energy and spin-orbit perturbation, they show that a current perpendicular to both the field and magnetization is produced. This current is proportional to the magnetization, offering a means to measure the latter directly. The magnitude of the Hall constant correlates with squared ordinary resistivity and temperature/impurity-resistant functions – findings in line with experimental results.

title: Observation of Resonance Condensation of Fermionic Atom Pairs
abstract: We have observed condensation of fermionic atom pairs in the BCS-BEC crossover regime. A trapped gas of fermionic 40K atoms is evaporatively cooled to quantum degeneracy and then a magnetic-field Feshbach resonance is used to control the atom-atom interactions. The location of this resonance is precisely determined from low-density measurements of molecule dissociation. In order to search for condensation on either side of the resonance, we introduce a technique that pairwise projects fermionic atoms onto molecules; this enables us to measure the momentum distribution of fermionic atom pairs. The transition to condensation of fermionic atom pairs is mapped out as a function of the initial atom gas temperature T compared to the Fermi temperature T(F) for magnetic-field detunings on both the BCS and BEC sides of the resonance.
summary:
New Study Observes Condensation of Atom Pairs in Quantum Physics Experiment

The study, published in Physical Review Letters, uses a magnetic-field Feshbach resonance to control the interactions of 40K atoms, paving the way for new research in quantum mechanics.

The scientists employ a novel technique to project fermionic atoms into molecules and measure their momentum distribution, providing unprecedented insights into condensation on both sides of the Feshbach resonance. The findings will contribute to a better understanding of complex quantum phenomena, furthering our knowledge in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Reverse Monte Carlo Simulation: A New Technique for the Determination of Disordered Structures
abstract: Abstract We have developed a new technique, based on the standard Monte Carlo simulation method with Markov chain sampling, in which a set of three dimensional particle configurations are generated that are consistent with the experimentally measured structure factor. A(Q), and radial distribution function, g(r), of a liquid or other disordered system. Consistency is determined by a standard χ2 test using the experimental errors. No input potential is required, we present initial results for liquid argon. Since the technique can work directly from the structure factor it promises to be useful for modelling the structures of glasses or amorphous materials. It also has other advantages in multicomponent systems and as a tool for experimental data analysis.

New Technique Unveiled: Reverse Monte Carlo Simulation for Analyzing Disordered Structures

Scientists R L McGreevy and László Pusztai have introduced a groundbreaking technique, the Reverse Monte Carlo Simulation, which could revolutionize the field of statistical physics. Initial findings for liquid argon show promising results, signalling the technique's potential for modeling structures in glasses, amorphous materials, multicomponent systems, and as a tool for experimental data analysis – opening new paths for understanding complex materials. title: Adsorption of<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">H</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">O</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math>,<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">N</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">H</mml:mi><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>, CO,<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">N</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">O</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>, and NO on graphene: A first-principles study
abstract: Motivated by the recent realization of graphene sensors to detect individual gas molecules, we investigate the adsorption of H2O, NH3, CO, NO2, and NO on a graphene substrate using first-principles calculations. The optimal adsorption position and orientation of these molecules on the graphene surface is determined and the adsorption energies are calculated. Molecular doping, i.e. charge transfer between the molecules and the graphene surface, is discussed in light of the density of states and the molecular orbitals of the adsorbates. The efficiency of doping of the different molecules is determined and the influence of their magnetic moment is discussed.
summary:
Title: New Insights into Graphene-Based Sensors: Study Reveals Adsorption Preferences

Journal: Physical Review B

In a groundbreaking study, scientists have explored the adsorption of various molecules - H2O, NH3, CO, NO and NO2 - on graphene as part of research into next-generation gas sensors capable of detecting individual molecules. The researchers employed first-principles calculations to identify the optimal positions and orientations of these molecules on graphene's surface, in turn calculating their adsorption energies.

The study also delves into molecular doping – the charge transfer between the adsorbates and the graphene surface – examining this phenomenon through the density of states and the molecular orbitals of the adsorbed molecules. The research sheds light on the efficiency of doping for these various molecules, and discusses the potential impact of their magnetic moments in the process.

title: Highly Efficient Multiple Exciton Generation in Colloidal PbSe and PbS Quantum Dots
abstract: We report ultra-efficient multiple exciton generation (MEG) for single photon absorption in colloidal PbSe and PbS quantum dots (QDs). We employ transient absorption spectroscopy and present measurement data acquired for both intraband as well as interband probe energies. Quantum yields of 300% indicate the creation, on average, of three excitons per absorbed photon for PbSe QDs at photon energies that are four times the QD energy gap. Results indicate that the threshold photon energy for MEG in QDs is twice the lowest exciton absorption energy. We find that the biexciton effect, which shifts the transition energy for absorption of a second photon, influences the early time transient absorption data and may contribute to a modulation observed when probing near the lowest interband transition. We present experimental and theoretical values of the size-dependent interband transition energies for PbSe QDs. We present experimental and theoretical values of the size-dependent interband transition energies for PbSe QDs, and we also introduce a new model for MEG based on the coherent superposition of multiple excitonic states.
summary:
**Research Breakthrough: Boosting Single Photon Absorption Efficiency in Quantum Dots**

Scientists, led by Randy J. Ellingson, have announced a significant breakthrough in the field of quantum dot technology. The researchers report ultra-efficient Multiple Exciton Generation (MEG) for single photon absorption in colloidal PbSe and PbS quantum dots, generating an average of three excitons per absorbed photon. This discovery could potentially enhance the efficiency of various optoelectronic devices, such as solar cells and LEDs.

The study suggests that the threshold photon energy for MEG in Quantum Dots is twice the lowest exciton absorption energy. The researchers also uncover the biexciton effect's influence on early time transient absorption data and propose a new model for MEG based on coherent superposition of multiple excitonic states. This work could pave the way for more advanced quantum dot applications and further research in this exciting field.

title: Topological Materials: Weyl Semimetals
abstract: Topological insulators and topological semimetals are both new classes of quantum materials, which are characterized by surface states induced by the topology of the bulk band structure. Topological Dirac or Weyl semimetals show linear dispersion around nodes, termed the Dirac or Weyl points, as the three-dimensional analog of graphene. We review the basic concepts and compare these topological states of matter from the materials perspective with a special focus on Weyl semimetals. The TaAs family is the ideal materials class to introduce the signatures of Weyl points in a pedagogical way, from Fermi arcs to the chiral magnetotransport properties, followed by hunting for the type-II Weyl semimetals in WTe 2 , MoTe 2 , and related compounds. Many materials are members of big families, and topological properties can be tuned. As one example, we introduce the multifunctional topological materials, Heusler compounds, in which both topological insulators and magnetic Weyl semimetals can be found. Instead of a comprehensive review, this article is expected to serve as a helpful introduction and summary by taking a snapshot of the quickly expanding field.
summary:
Headline: "New Class of Quantum Materials Unearthed: Topological Weyl Semimetals"

Summary:
In a new review published in Annals of Condensed Matter Physics, researchers Binghai Yan and Claudia Felser delve into the world of topological materials, specifically spotlighting Weyl semimetals. These materials, characterized by surface states and three-dimensional linear dispersions called Weyl points, are seen as the three-dimensional analog of graphene. The authors highlight the TaAs family as an ideal starting point to understand the signatures of Weyl points, including Fermi arcs and chiral magnetotransport properties. Furthermore, the review explores the potential of finding type-II Weyl semimetals in WTe2, MoTe2, and related compounds. The researchers also introduce multifunctional topological materials, Heusler compounds, where both topological insulators and magnetic Weyl semimetals can be found. The work aims to provide a comprehensive but easy-to-understand introduction to this rapidly expanding field of topological quantum materials.

title: Massive Dirac Fermions and Hofstadter Butterfly in a van der Waals Heterostructure
abstract: Graphene, Gapped and Butterflied The remarkable transport properties of graphene, such as the high electron mobility, make it a promising material for electronics. However, unlike semiconductors such as silicon, graphene's electronic structure lacks a band gap, and a transistor made out of graphene would not have an “off” state. Hunt et al. (p. 1427 , published online 16 May; see the Perspective by Fuhrer ) modulated the electronic properties of graphene by building a heterostructure consisting of a graphene flake resting on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), which has the same honeycomb structure as graphene, but consists of alternating boron and nitrogen atoms instead of carbons. The natural mismatch between the graphene and hBN lattices led to a moire pattern with a large wavelength, causing the opening of a band gap, the formation of an elusive fractional quantum Hall state, and, at high magnetic fields, a fractal phenomenon in the electronic structure called the Hofstadter butterfly.
summary:
Scientific Discovery Opens New Possibilities for Graphene-Based Electronics

In a groundbreaking new study published in Science, researchers led by Benjamin Hunt have managed to open a band gap and create a unique electronic structure – known as the Hofstadter butterfly – in graphene. This discovery represents an important step forward in the quest for next-generation electronics using this versatile material.

To achieve this result, the team applied a novel approach involving the creation of a heterostructure consisting of a single layer of graphene deposited on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), another honeycomb lattice material. By leveraging the lattice mismatch between these two materials, the researchers induced a moire pattern with a large wavelength that led to the opening of a band gap and the formation of a fractional quantum Hall state at low magnetic fields, as well as the emergence of the elusive Hofstadter butterfly at high magnetic fields.

This work offers exciting perspectives for future research in condensed matter physics and could pave the way for the development of innovative graphene-based electronic devices that feature an "off" state, previously unattainable with conventional graphene materials.

title: Hydrophobicity at Small and Large Length Scales
abstract: We develop a unified and generally applicable theory of solvation of small and large apolar species in water. In the former, hydrogen bonding of water is hindered yet persists near the solutes. In the latter, hydrogen bonding is depleted, leading to drying of extended apolar surfaces, large forces of attraction, and hysteresis on mesoscopic length scales. The crossover occurs on nanometer length scales, when the local concentration of apolar units is sufficiently high, or when an apolar surface is sufficiently large. Our theory for the crossover has implications concerning the stability of protein assemblies and protein folding.
summary:
Scientists Develop New Theory on Water's Interaction with Apolar Species

In a new study published in The Journal of Physical Chemistry B, researchers led by Ka Lum, David Chandler, and John D. Weeks have proposed a unifying theory for the solvation of small and large apolar species in water. The theory explains how hydrogen bonding in water, though hindered near small solutes, persists, and how it is depleted on larger scales, leading to attraction and hysteresis on the mesoscopic level.

The research sheds light on a crossover phenomenon occurring on a nanometer scale, where the local concentration of apolar units determines whether hydrogen bonding continues or becomes depleted. The team's findings could have implications for understanding protein assemblies and protein folding stability.

title: Liquid Crystals
abstract: This is a new and greatly revised edition of Professor Chandrasekhar's classic book Liquid Crystals, first published in 1977. The subject of liquid crystals has grown into an exciting interdisciplinary research field with important practical applications. This book presents a systematic and self-contained treatment of the physics of the different types of thermotropic liquid crystals - the three classical types, nematic, cholesteric and smectic, and the newly discovered discotic type. Included is a description of the structures of these four main types and their polymorphic modifications, their thermodynamical, optical and mechanical properties and their behaviour under external fields. The basic principles underlying the major applications of liquid crystals in display technology and in thermography are also discussed. This book will be of great value to advanced students and researchers in condensed matter physics, chemical physics, materials science and technology with an interest in the physics, chemistry and applications of liquid crystals.

Headline:
Revised Edition of "Liquid Crystals" Highlights Growth of Interdisciplinary Field

In a new edition of his classic book, Professor S. Chandrasekhar delves into the updated world of liquid crystals, an interdisciplinary research field that has surged since its debut in 1977 with important practical applications. The revised text covers the physics of four main types of thermotropic liquid crystals, including nematic, cholesteric, smectic, and discotic varieties, along with their unique structures, properties, and behaviors under various external fields. This self-contained book aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and advanced students in physics, chemistry, materials science, and technology, especially those interested in the physics, chemistry, and applications of liquid crystals, particularly in display technology and thermography.

title: Ferroelectricity in Simple Binary ZrO<sub>2</sub> and HfO<sub>2</sub>
abstract: The transition metal oxides ZrO(2) and HfO(2) as well as their solid solution are widely researched and, like most binary oxides, are expected to exhibit centrosymmetric crystal structure and therewith linear dielectric characteristics. For this reason, those oxides, even though successfully introduced into microelectronics, were never considered to be more than simple dielectrics possessing limited functionality. Here we report the discovery of a field-driven ferroelectric phase transition in pure, sub 10 nm ZrO(2) thin films and a composition- and temperature-dependent transition to a stable ferroelectric phase in the HfO(2)-ZrO(2) mixed oxide. These unusual findings are attributed to a size-driven tetragonal to orthorhombic phase transition that in thin films, similar to the anticipated tetragonal to monoclinic transition, is lowered to room temperature. A structural investigation revealed the orthorhombic phase to be of space group Pbc2(1), whose noncentrosymmetric nature is deemed responsible for the spontaneous polarization in this novel, nanoscale ferroelectrics.
summary:
New Study Uncovers Unexpected Ferroelectric Properties in Common Materials

Scientists have discovered that common materials ZrO2 and HfO2 — often used in microelectronics and thought to be simple insulators — can exhibit ferroelectric properties, a surprising development with potential implications for future technology.

The research team from the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg found that when these materials are made into thin layers thinner than 10 nanometers, they undergo an unusual phase transition at room temperature. In the case of ZrO2, the change leads to spontaneous polarization never before observed in this material. Meanwhile, a HfO2-ZrO2 mix can transform into a stable ferroelectric phase due to specific composition and temperature conditions. These findings could expand the understanding and applications of these materials in various electronic devices.

Halperin in 1982. The research explores the interplay between these concepts to gain insights into the properties and behavior of such systems.

**Scientific Findings: New Insights Into Two-Dimensional Disordered Potential**

A new study published in the reputable physics journal, Physical Review B, delves into the mysterious world of two-dimensional disordered potential and offers fresh perspectives on quantized Hall conductance, current-carrying edge states, and extended states. The groundbreaking work by physicist Bertrand I. Halperin provides vital insights into the properties and behavior of such systems, building upon earlier research in condensed matter physics. title: Colossal magnetoresistance
abstract: We review recent experimental work falling under the broad classification of colossal magnetoresistance (CMR), which is magnetoresistance associated with a ferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic phase transition. The prototypical CMR compound is derived from the parent compound, perovskite . When hole doped at a concentration of 20 - 40% holes/Mn ion, for instance by Ca or Sr substitution for La, the material displays a transition from a high-temperature paramagnetic insulator to a low-temperature ferromagnetic metal. Near the phase transition temperature, which can exceed room temperature in some compositions, large magnetoresistance is observed and its possible application in magnetic recording has revived interest in these materials. In addition, unusual magneto-elastic effects and charge ordering have focused attention on strong electron - phonon coupling. This coupling, which is a type of dynamic extended-system version of the Jahn - Teller effect, in conjunction with the double-exchange interaction, is also viewed as essential for a microscopic description of CMR in the manganite perovskites. Large magnetoresistance is also seen in other systems, namely and some Cr chalcogenide spinels, compounds which differ greatly from the manganite perovskites. We describe the relevant points of contrast between the various CMR materials.
summary:
"Colossal Magnetoresistance (CMR) Gains Momentum in Condensed Matter Physics"

In a recent paper published in Journal of Physics Condensed Matter, researcher A.P. Ramirez reviews the growing field of colossal magnetoresistance (CMR). The study focuses on materials derived from the perovskite compound, where doping with 20-40% holes leads to a transition from paramagnetic insulator to a ferromagnetic metal that exhibits large magnetoresistance, which could potentially revolutionize magnetic recording.

In addition to manganite perovskites, CMR is also observed in other systems such as cuprates and Cr chalcogenide spinels. Understanding the unique characteristics and differences between these diverse groups of materials continues to be a subject of intense interest within the physics community.
topic: Magnetic and transport properties of perovskites and related materials
